I. INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND 
The history of Raman scattering can be traced back to 1928, when Indian physicist C.V. Raman published the groundbreaking article, A New Type of Secondary Radiation, in Nature. 1 What is less well-known is that the phenomenon of Raman scattering had been predicted earlier by Austrian physicist Adolf Smekal in 1923.2 He correctly assigned the frequency shift between the incident and scattered light to the energy difference between the two states of the molecule. Since its advent, Raman scattering has been recognized as an extremely weak process, and it did not gain widespread use until the development of high-power lasers in the 1960s, finding applications in chemical and material analysis.3,4 
The process described above is typically referred to as spontaneous Raman scattering, in contrast to stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) (Fig. 1). SRS was serendipitously discovered in 1962 by 
Woodbury and $\mathrm { N g } ,$ who observed an unexpected laser wavelength shift in a Ruby laser caused by the Stokes scattering of nitrobenzene.5,6 
The phenomenon of SRS carries the spirit of stimulated emission, where the rate of Raman scattering is amplified by the introduction of the Stokes beam, whose energy difference with respect to the pump beam matches that of the vibrational energy of the sample. Initially, SRS was mainly used as Raman-based shifter and Raman lasers around 1960 and $1 9 7 0 \mathrm { { \dot { s } } ^ { 6 - 1 1 } }$ due to the new radiation generated. Its subsequent applications in time-resolved spectroscopy such as impulsive SRS (ISRS) and femtosecond SRS (FSRS) since 1980s were leveraging the ultrafast nature of the excitation pulses.12–16 While the coherent radiation and time-resolved nature have been readily appreciated as the advantages of SRS over the spontaneous counterpart, SRS was not implemented for sensitive detection for most part of the history. 
A breakthrough occurred in late 2008 and early 2009, when SRS was implemented with high-speed lock-in detection and laser scanning microscopy, enabling rapid, high-sensitivity vibrational imaging.17–20 By detecting the energy transfer between the laser and the molecule, SRS microscopy was developed mostly as an alternative to coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy.21 Superseding CARS microscopy in almost all aspects, this innovation sparkled a fast-growing field at the intersection of optics, chemistry, life science and engineering.20,22–24 At its inception, SRS microscopy was a labelfree imaging modality with extensive effort devoted to improving the speed, resolution, and sensitivity through clever engineering and instrument design.25–41 The concurrent development of vibrational probes further fueled SRS imaging capabilities. In particular, small molecules tagged with bio-orthogonal isotopes and triple bonds allow for chemical-specific imaging in live cell and tissues.42–45 Two palettes of dyes, MARS and Carbow, were created to allow for ultra-sensitive, supermultiplexed vibrational imaging.46,47 Further efforts on developing photo-activatable and photo-switchable dyes are also fruitful.48–51 

These new probes have found applications in many fields of research, including metabolic imaging in cells and animals, drug discovery, functional sensing and profiling, amongst others.52–56 
However just why can SRS microscopy outperform spontaneous Raman microscopy under comparable imaging conditions? This might appear to be a strange or even ironic question to ask, given the significant technology advancements made in the past 15 years. The fact is that the field of SRS microscopy is mostly driven empirically. To our best knowledge, SRS microscopy was not rigorously proved or predicted to be superior to spontaneous Raman microscopy by 2008; even more than a decade after its invention, the core question regarding the sensitivity comparison had remained challenging to address quantitatively; until recently, there has been no straightforward way of predicting numerical values of SRS rates and signal level. Hence, the very foundation for why one needs to perform SRS microscopy has not been firmly established. Just like the SRS effect is a serendipitous discovery in history, the development of SRS microscopy is largely empirical in nature. 
In this review, we summarize the recently developed stimulated response formulation of Raman scattering.57–61 We begin by defining a new property, stimulated Raman cross section, $\sigma _ { \scriptstyle \mathrm { S R S } } ,$ phenomenologically, to reflect the intrinsic molecular response under SRS. Surprisingly, $\sigma _ { \scriptstyle \mathrm { S R S } }$ is comparable, or even exceed its electronic counterpart of two-photon absorption (TPA), ${ \sigma } _ { \mathrm { T P A } } ,$ a reversal of the conventional paradigm for the linear case ${ \sigma _ { \mathrm { U V - V i s } } }$ vs $\sigma _ { \mathrm { R a m a n } } )$ .57 We then establish a connection equation for $\sigma _ {  { \mathrm { S R S } } }$ and $\sigma _ { \mathrm { R a m a n } }$ heuristically without invoking full quantum mechanics. The key insight is to regard spontaneous Raman scattering as a special case of SRS, where the Stokes energy is supplied by vacuum zero-point fluctuation.58 We then provide a full quantum electrodynamics treatment for $\sigma _ { \scriptstyle \mathrm { S R S } }$ and compare it to the expression of $\sigma _ { \mathrm { R a m a n } } ,$ which fully recover the connection equation.59 This dual behavior of being weak and strong simultaneously prompted us to propose “the duality of Raman scattering,” which in turn generalizes Einstein’s coefficients to include four processes (spontaneous and stimulated emission, spontaneous and stimulated Raman scattering).61 Finally, we show that the duality notion can help establish a quantitative treatment of SRS microscopy, resolving long-standing debates about detection sensitivity.60 A twodimensional phase-diagram-like graph can depict the fundamental detectability for both spontaneous Raman scattering and SRS. This new formulation, thus, unravels new insights of Raman scattering, lays a modern theoretical foundation for SRS microscopy, and promises to facilitate its future progress.

3ba293d44447_fine_1: [Content] In 1999, my group reported a novel CARS microscope with raster scanning two collinear laser beams at near-infrared wavelengths [5]. This method greatly simplified the instrumentation, offered biocompatibility, and triggered a series of innovations, broad applications, and commercialization of CARS microscopy. Many advances on CARS microscopy were accounted in a book published by CRC Press in 2012 [6]. Unfortunately, the CARS signal is accompanied by a nonresonant background, which greatly reduces vibrational contrast, especially for fingerprint Raman bands. SRS, which is a dissipative process involving energy transfer from laser fields to molecules, avoids the nonresonant background and offers quantitative contrast. The first SRS microscope reported in 2007 was based on multiplexed detection of signals generated by high-energy pulses [7]. However, low repetition rate of the laser system and low dynamic range of its acquisition system drastically reduced signal-to-noise ratio and resulted in a pixel dwell time on the second scale. In 2008, my group reported a high-speed SRS microscope suitable for biological imaging [8], in which shot-noise-limited detection was achieved based on laser intensity modulation at MHz rate and phasesensitive lock-in amplifier detection. This work together with studies by other groups have led SRS microscopy become a powerful tool for basic research as well as translational medicine. The current book on techniques and applications of SRS microscopy, edited by Ji-Xin Cheng, Wei Min, Yasuyuki Ozeki, and Dario Polli, is rather comprehensive. In the first part, researchers describe the history of SRS and the theory, sensitivity, and noise in SRS microscopy. The second part describes various instrumentation strategies that pushed the physical limits of SRS microscopy such as detection sensitivity, spatial resolution, imaging speed, and penetration depth. The third part explores the development of vibrational probes, which dramatically increased the sensitivity, specificity, and functionality in SRS imaging. The fourth part presents data science methods developed for decomposing a hyperspectral SRS image into chemical maps, compressive sensing, and denoising. The fifth part illustrates a broad spectrum of applications enabled by SRS microscopy. The final part is devoted to most recent efforts in miniaturization and translation to medicine. It is truly exciting and rewarding to see the breadth and the depth of these developments and applications.

In 2008, my group reported a high-speed SRS microscope suitable for biological imaging [8], in which shot-noise-limited detection was achieved based on laser intensity modulation at MHz rate and phasesensitive lock-in amplifier detection. This work together with studies by other groups have led SRS microscopy become a powerful tool for basic research as well as translational medicine. The current book on techniques and applications of SRS microscopy, edited by Ji-Xin Cheng, Wei Min, Yasuyuki Ozeki, and Dario Polli, is rather comprehensive. In the first part, researchers describe the history of SRS and the theory, sensitivity, and noise in SRS microscopy. The second part describes various instrumentation strategies that pushed the physical limits of SRS microscopy such as detection sensitivity, spatial resolution, imaging speed, and penetration depth. The third part explores the development of vibrational probes, which dramatically increased the sensitivity, specificity, and functionality in SRS imaging. The fourth part presents data science methods developed for decomposing a hyperspectral SRS image into chemical maps, compressive sensing, and denoising. The fifth part illustrates a broad spectrum of applications enabled by SRS microscopy. The final part is devoted to most recent efforts in miniaturization and translation to medicine. It is truly exciting and rewarding to see the breadth and the depth of these developments and applications.

DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION 
As we discussed in the Background, SRS was not considered as a sensitive detection method in most of the history, and the invention and subsequent development of SRS microscopy were not based on rigorous prediction. These become readily justified in retrospect, as our theoretical analysis has proven that SRS spectroscopy (typically done with large volume and long time) does not provide better detection sensitivity than conventional Raman spectroscopy. Our analysis further shows that SRS can surpass the fundamental detection limit of spontaneous Raman scattering but only in the high spatiotemporal limits. This perfectly explains why SRS has become significant and appreciated only in the era of biological imaging of the 21th century. As bioimaging was advancing into higher spatial resolution and faster temporal resolution, SRS has become an inevitable choice in the domain of Raman microscopy. Furthermore, it also forecasts its future impact, as even higher spatiotemporal resolutions are being pursued. 

Our finding underscores a principle that has not been explicitly articulated before: stimulated transition can exceed the sensitivity of the spontaneous counterpart even in the ideal background-free scenario. Recall that the fundamental detection limit (eq 4) of spontaneous Raman scattering is derived without any background or detector noise. This insight about Raman scattering could be surprising especially when viewed together with the overwhelming success of fluorescence microscopy operating on the opposite principle—spontaneous emission is generally more sensitive than the stimulated emission (or stimulated absorption). In our opinion, these two seemingly opposite conclusions between Raman scattering and light emission are not contradictory to each other but rather are two valid consequences at distinct parameter spaces. 
Another somewhat counterintuitive insight is that SRS spectroscopy and SRS microscopy, despite both being based on the same underlying SRS optical process, rely on different principles and purposes. When SRS was utilized for spectroscopic studies, it is not meant or designed to be a sensitive detection tool but rather an optical science tool to study various ultrafast (time-resolved) and physical processes that is otherwise not achievable by spontaneous Raman scattering. In this sense, SRS microscopy should not be considered as a natural extension of SRS spectroscopy. In fact, SRS spectroscopy is more similar to stimulated emission spectroscopy, which has been utilized to study nonfluorescent molecules and the lifetime of electronic excited states and hand, is based on an entirely different principle to achieve unprecedented speed and sensitivity compared to spontaneous Raman microscopy methods.

[Subsection] Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) is the most widely used non-linear Raman process. For SRS, two synchronized lasers are used as the pump laser and the Stokes laser. When the energy difference between the pump and the Stokes lasers matches the energy required for molecular vibration excitation, the molecules are coherently excited to a higher vibrational level (Fig. 1b) The signal is detected as intensity gain (Stokes) or intensity loss (pump) The Raman shift observed in SRS, i.e., the frequency difference between the pump and Stokes, and the spontaneous Raman shift are the same for a molecule. Since it is a resonantly enhanced process, SRS gives much stronger signal in a shorter time compared to spontaneous Raman. Though advantageous over spontaneous Raman imaging with respect to acquisition time, SRS requires a complex ultrafast laser setup. Xie and co-workers pioneered the Raman imaging of biological samples using non-linear modes. Using SRS microscopy, they were able to image the uptake of omega-3 fatty acid by A549 lung cells, visualize neuron bundles in mouse tissue, and monitor the delivery of retinoic acid in mouse skin.22 In another modification called spectrally tailored excitation SRS, the pump pulse is tailored to collectively excite all vibrational modes of the target molecules. This technique was used to image protein, oleic acid, and stearic acid in C. elegans. 23 
SRS microscopy has been used to visualize DNA in cells and in mouse skin, to visualize lipids in human skin, to monitor early peripheral nervous degeneration in mouse and drug delivery in fresh mouse skin, and even to detect neuronal membrane potential.24–28 Ozeki and coworkers demonstrated its applicability in plant cell imaging.29 Min and coworkers combined tissue-clearing methods with SRS to obtain a 10 times greater imaging depth than could be achieved in regular SRS imaging. This enabled 3D imaging of tumor spheroids, mouse brain tissues, and tumor xenografts. By applying volumetric phasor analysis, they were also able to extract quantitative information on the distribution of blood vessels, axon fibers, and cell bodies in various brain regions.30 One of the most innovative and exciting developments is label-free flow cytometry and cell sorting, achieved by integration of these techniques with SRS imaging.31,32

[Abstract] Abstract 
Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) describes a family of techniques first discovered and developed in the 1960s. Whereas the nascent history of the technique is parallel to that of laser light sources, recent advances have spurred a resurgence in its use and development that has spanned across scientific fields and spatial scales. SRS is a nonlinear technique that probes the same vibrational modes of molecules that are seen in spontaneous Raman scattering. While spontaneous Raman scattering is an incoherent technique, SRS is a coherent process, and this fact provides several advantages over conventional Raman techniques, among which are much stronger signals and the ability to time-resolve the vibrational motions. Technological improvements in pulse generation and detection strategies have allowed SRS to probe increasingly smaller volumes and shorter time scales. This has enabled SRS research to move from its original domain, of probing bulk media, to imaging biological tissues and single cells at the micro scale, and, ultimately, to characterizing samples with subdiffraction resolution at the nanoscale. In this Review, we give an overview of the history of the technique, outline its basic properties, and present historical and current uses at multiple length scales to underline the utility of SRS to the molecular sciences.

1. Introduction 
Raman spectroscopy is based on Raman scattering,[1] which results from energy exchange between an incident photon and the molecular vibrational or rotational level. Since every molecule has unique energy levels and the frequency of scattered light from a molecule can describe the structural characteristics of its chemical bonds, Raman spectroscopy enables highly chemical-specific, high-sensitivity, and high-accuracy analysis of molecular vibration modes. By combining Raman spectroscopy and microscopy, spontaneous Raman scattering microscopy was proposed to selectively image unique chemical components according to the Raman spectra of various molecules without the need for an exogenous label.[2] Therefore, Raman scattering microscopy has been explored for biomedical applications to image the chemical composition of cells and tissues and assess cell cycle dynamics, cell differentiation, cell death,[3] cancers of various organs, and diagnosis of certain vascular diseases.[4] Nevertheless, spontaneous Raman scattering is a feeble process (one inelastically scattered photon for every $\mathrm { \bar { 1 0 ^ { 7 } } }$ elastically scattered photons) featuring time-consuming spectral integration and hence a poor acquisition speed (several seconds per line or minutes per frame). This weakness constitutes a large obstacle for real-time monitoring of dynamic events in organisms. 

Recently, several variations of Raman spectroscopy have been developed to enhance the sensitivity of Raman spectroscopy and dynamic processes of biological samples, including coherent Raman scattering (CRS) spectroscopy and surfaceenhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS). SERS involves a plasmonic effect where molecules absorbed on a rough metal surface can result in high Raman scattering intensities by increasing the incident electric field.[5] For SERS technology, a SERS substrate must be introduced to enhance the detection sensitivity, and the properties of the substrate (the composition, size, shape and aggregation degree of nanoparticles) affect the shape of the SERS spectra. In addition, only gold, silver, copper, and a few rare alkali metals (such as lithium and sodium) have strong SERS effects, and it is necessary to effectively solve the biocompatibility and safety issues in the preparation of nanomaterials. With the development of laser and nonlinear optics, CRS microscopy has also been demonstrated to break the speed limit for vibrational imaging.[6] CRS has two major forms: coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) and stimulated Raman scattering (SRS);7] both techniques can dramatically increase the Raman signal by a few orders of magnitude and hence are able to achieve video-rate molecular imaging in vivo.[8,9] 

CARS and SRS processes often exist in a sample concurrently because of the same excitation conditions (spatiotemporal overlap of the pump and Stokes beam) with a frequency difference (Raman shift) matching the molecular vibrational frequency. However, CARS is an optical parametric process accompanied by a nonresonant part originating from fourwave mixing processes. This intrinsic nonresonant background results in a deviation or even distortion of the Raman spectrum. SRS is a direct process of photon-vibration energy transfer: in brief, the interaction between the electron cloud of a sample and the photons of two lasers creates an induced dipole moment within the molecule based on its polarizability, resulting in a pump energy loss (stimulated Raman loss, SRL) and a Stokes energy increase (stimulated Raman gain, SRG). The Raman signal can, therefore, be deduced from SRL or SRG, resulting in a high-fidelity Raman spectrum free from the nonresonant background. Moreover, the SRS signal exhibits a linear correlation between the signal intensity and the specimen concentration, facilitating straightforward component and concentration analysis of the sample without spectral-distortion correction. 

Since the first practical SRS microscopy technique was proposed with a modulated picosecond pulse and lock-in detection and applied in biomedical imaging,[10] the SRS microscopic technique has undergone extensive research and development. The advantages of typical SRS microscopy include 1) low phototoxicity and photobleaching because of nonfluorescence imaging; 2) video-rate imaging speed, in contrast to spontaneous Raman microscopy; 3) use of a near-infrared (NIR) laser source to achieve depth imaging without severe photodamage to biological tissues; 4) quantitative vibrational imaging with high sensitivity and accuracy; and 5) compatibility with other imaging technologies. In this paper, we will introduce the principle and instrumentation of SRS microscopy, scrutinize the pros and cons of different experimental designs, discuss the imaging speed, SNR, and other performance parameters of SRS, and eventually focus on its applications in the life sciences. 
Technique and Method Development 
Principle and Modalities of SRS Microscopy 
Typically, the critical components of an SRS microscopy system include two synchronized pulse lasers, an optical modulator, a scanning microscope, and a demodulator, which are illustrated in Figure 1a. Regarding the principle of SRS, two incoming fields at a pump frequency $w _ { \mathrm { p } }$ and Stokes frequency $\omega _ { \mathrm { s } }$ excite the sample. When the difference frequency of the two beams, $\Delta \omega = \omega _ { \mathrm { p } } - \omega _ { \mathrm { s } }$ , matches the vibration frequency of the molecule, $\Omega$ , the molecule population is transferred from the ground state through a virtual state to the vibrationally excited state. As a result of stimulated excitation of the molecular transition, the molecular transition rate is enhanced in contrast to that in spontaneous Raman. Due to the coherent excitation of molecular vibration, a pump photon is absorbed by the sample, and a Stokes photon is generated, which results in a loss (SRL) and gain (SRG), resulting in intensity changes in the pump and Stokes beams, $\Delta I _ { \mathrm { P } }$ and $\Delta I _ { \mathrm { s } }$ . In an SRS instrument, the pump and Stokes beams are spatially and temporally overlapped by a dichroic mirror and a delay positioning system, respectively, directed to the scanning microscope and focused onto the specimen with an objective lens. The SRS signal is collected by a condenser, passes through the filter, and then detected with a photodiode. This signal is represented by the intensity change of the incident laser $( \Delta I _ { \mathrm { P } } / I _ { \mathrm { P } }$ or $\Delta I _ { \mathrm { s } } / I _ { \mathrm { s } } , \approx 1 0 ^ { - 3 } – 1 0 ^ { - 7 } )$ , which is so small that it can easily be lost in noise. Thus, a well-known mechanism referred to as "modulation-demodulation" is introduced to extract the tiny signal from the high laser intensity while suppressing the laser, thermal, and shot noise. One of the excitation beams (mostly Stokes) is modulated by an acousto-optic modulator (AOM) or an electro-optic modulator (EOM) with high frequency before entering the microscope. Then, the intensity of the other beam is detected through one or more filters with high optical density $\mathrm { ( O D > 6 ) }$ to filter out the modulated light. The $\operatorname { S R G } /$ SRL signals buried in the high-laser-intensity background can, therefore, be demodulated using a lock-in amplifier based on the modulation function and shown graphically. 

To acquire pixelwise Raman spectra, a variety of approaches to scan Raman frequency shifts in sequence or parallel have been proposed, which can be divided into three groups: sequential wavelength tuning, spectral focusing, and parallel multiplex excitation and detection. For wavelength tuning (Figure 1b), frequency shift scanning is achieved by changing the wavelength of a tunable laser while maintaining the wavelength of a narrowband laser. This method usually utilizes at least one picosecond-pulse laser, taking advantage of its narrowband feature to achieve hyperspectral measurements (several to dozens of wavenumbers). However, the Raman shift is usually obtained by changing the nonlinear crystal temperature, electro-optical Lyot filter or resonator length[,]o the asr, featurin a so speal acquisition speed and low nonlinear optical intensity. For compatibility with femtosecond lasers to achieve hyperspectral Raman imaging, the pulse shaping method has been proposed to narrow the bandwidth laser and rapidly scan the Raman shift.typical pulse-haping configuratio consists of a folded 4f pulse shaper, formed by a gating, an chromatic lens, a reflector, a splitter, and an electric translation platform. The incident beam is spectrally separated by the grating and focused at the Fourier plane of the achromatic lens. The adjustable slit and reflector are also placed at the Fourier plane on the electric translation platform. A sufficiently narrow slit can leak out a small part of the laser with a cut bandwidth to achieve high spectral resolution. However, this method complicates the SRS system and requires a relatively high laser energy because only a small fequency range is used at a pixel point. Spectral focusing based on two femtosecond lasers (Figure 1c) is another approach to achieve a narrow Raman bandwidth. In this setup, both laser pulses are positively chirped by glasses, prisms, gratings, or other dispersion materials to accomplish a linear distribution of spectral frequency on the time axis.

1. INTRODUCTION 
The moniker stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) encompasses a collection of optical techniques that share in common a light–matter interaction in which two light fields induce a Raman-active transition in the material. Since the 1960s, these techniques have been used extensively to study the vibrational properties of gases, liquids, and solids. A nonlinear optical technique, SRS is sensitive to the same molecular vibrations that are probed in spontaneous Raman scattering.1 These vibrational modes include vibrational motions of individual chemical bonds and chemical groups, and thus form a means to not only identify molecules but also study their structural dynamics and probe their intra- and intermolecular interactions. Although SRS and spontaneous Raman scattering are fundamentally related, there are important differences between the two techniques. As compared to spontaneous Raman scattering, in which the light-induced molecular motions in the sample are incoherent, in SRS the vibrational modes are prepared in a coherent fashion. With all modes oscillating in unison, forming a coherent polarization in the sample, the subsequent radiation derived from the polarization is also coherent. The resulting SRS radiation is highly directional and strong, offering signal detection efficiencies that are many orders of magnitude higher than in spontaneous Raman scattering. In addition, SRS techniques enable the direct observation of the coherent molecular motions at ultrafast time scales, following their evolution and dephasing as a function of time. This allows a time-ordered view of processes and molecular dynamics that cannot always be directly inferred from an analysis of the Raman spectrum alone. These two advantages, the strong Raman-sensitive signals and the ability to time-resolve molecular motions, have defined SRS as an important tool in chemistry, biophysics, and biomolecular imaging. 
The impact of SRS in the molecular sciences has changed over time, and is still changing today. The development of the technique is intimately linked to the evolution of laser light sources, as we will briefly review below. With the steady advances in laser pulse generation and light detection technologies, the sensitivity of SRS has improved markedly over the years, allowing the registration of molecules at lower concentrations and in smaller sample volumes. Whereas earlier applications of SRS focused on the study of pure liquids or highly concentrated molecular targets, improvements in sensitivity are driving applications into the direction of heterogeneous microstructured samples, individual nanoscopic objects, and, ultimately, single molecules. In this Review, we describe how developments in SRS have enabled the transition from bulk samples to nanostructured samples of chemical relevance. 
We discuss the properties of SRS in the context of these developments and highlight the impact that the technique has had in various fields of research.

INTRODUCTION 
The moniker stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) encompasses a collection of optical techniques that share in common a light—matter interaction in which two light fields induce a Raman-active transition in the material. Since the 1960s, these techniques have been used extensively to study the vibrational properties of gases, liquids, and solids. A nonlinear optical technique, SRS is sensitive to the same molecular vibrations that are probed in spontaneous Raman scattering.1 These vibrational modes include vibrational motions of individual chemical bonds and chemical groups, and thus form a means to not only identify molecules but also study their structural dynamics and probe their intra- and intermolecular interactions. Although SRS and spontaneous Raman scattering are fundamentally related, there are important differences between the two techniques. As compared to spontaneous Raman scattering, in which the light-induced molecular motions in the sample are incoherent, in SRS the vibrational modes are prepared in a coherent fashion. With all modes oscillating in unison, forming a coherent polarization in the sample, the subsequent radiation derived from the polarization is also coherent. The resulting SRS radiation is highly directional and strong, offering signal detection efficiencies that are many orders of magnitude higher than in spontaneous Raman scattering. In addition, SRS techniques enable the direct observation of the coherent molecular motions at ultrafast time scales, following their evolution and dephasing as a function of time. This allows a time-ordered view of processes and molecular dynamics that cannot always be directly inferred from an analysis of the Raman spectrum alone. These two advantages, the strong Raman-sensitive signals and the ability to time-resolve molecular motions, have defined SRS as an important tool in chemistry, biophysics, and biomolecular imaging. 

The impact of SRS in the molecular sciences has changed over time, and is still changing today. The development of the technique is intimately linked to the evolution of laser light sources, as we will briefly review below. With the steady advances in laser pulse generation and light detection technologies, the sensitivity of SRS has improved markedly over the years, allowing the registration of molecules at lower concentrations and in smaller sample volumes. Whereas earlier applications of SRS focused on the study of pure liquids or highly concentrated molecular targets, improvements in sensitivity are driving applications into the direction of heterogeneous microstructured samples, individual nanoscopic objects, and, ultimately, single molecules. In this Review, we describe how developments in SRS have enabled the transition from bulk samples to nanostructured samples of chemical relevance. We discuss the properties of SRS in the context of these developments and highlight the impact that the technique has had in various fields of research.

Notable innovations include video-rate imaging, single-molecule vibrational imaging, super-resolution SRS, hyperspectral SRS, and quantumenhanced SRS, among others.4159 Vibrational probes provide another wave of applications of metabolic imaging, supermultiplexed imaging, and vibrational sensing to address biological complexity.9,6072 Going beyond biomedical applications, SRS microscopy also finds broad impact on materials science, battery research, drug development, and environmental science.29,7377 
Despite its remarkable success, both the invention and the subsequent development of SRS microscopy are driven more empirically than rationally. A few careful reflections support this assessment. First, the notion of choosing SRS microscopy over its spontaneous counterpart is contrary to conventional wisdom. As single-molecule fluorescence spectroscopy and microscopy have transformed analytical chemistry and optical microscopy in the late 1990s, the chemistry community has long embraced the notion of background-free detection.7880 As a result, when it comes to sensitive detection of light emission, background-free spontaneous emission (i.e., fluorescence) is almost always favored over stimulated emission. Similarly, when it comes to light scattering, few would have conceptually predicted that SRS's sensitivity could surpass spontaneous Raman, which is theoretically background-free. Indeed, in addition to rate enhancements, SRS introduces additional laser intensity noise, unlike the "noise-free" nature of spontaneous Raman. Thus, enhanced "stimulated" rate in SRS does not necessarily translate to improved sensitivity, which explains why SRS was not regarded by spectroscopists for sensitive detection in most of the history.

BACKGROUND 
Imaging techniques facilitate scientific advancement by monitoring the changing world with spatial and temporal information. Recognized by multiple Nobel prizes in recent decades, cutting-edge imaging techniques have revolutionized one's ability to visualize the unseen.1-3 Scientists have leveraged numerous contrasting mechanisms to expose the hidden world, resulting in advanced techniques such as fluorescence microscopy, electron microscopy, atomic force microscopy, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging. Among the myriad imaging techniques, chemical imaging, which harnesses chemical bonds as the imaging target, has emerged as a popular approach in recent years.4 Chemical bonding is a fundamental concept across many disciplines, making chemical imaging broadly applicable in biomedicine, material science, and fundamental physics. The most prominent chemical imaging methods include infrared (IR) absorption and Raman scattering. Of the two, Raman scattering has been proven to be impactful in biological applications due to its desirable features: it is free from water background, compatible with live cells, and capable of volumetric imaging with high resolution. 
Discovered by Indian physicist C.V. Raman in 1928,8 the Raman scattering effect refers to the nonelastic scattering of photons caused by interaction of light and matter, which is also commonly referred to as the spontaneous Raman scattering. The scattered Raman photons carry rich chemical information about the sample, including the nature of the chemical bond, abundance, local environment, etc. Despite its promise, spontaneous Raman is often criticized as being an extremely weak process due to the very small probability of scattering events, with cross sections up to $1 0 ^ { 1 \bar { 4 } }$ times smaller than the Raman microscopy typically takes hours, if not days, to acquire a three-dimensional biological image of a reasonable size, preventing its wide application in biomedical research. While recent progress in the development of line-scan Raman microscopy has reduced such scanning time to ${ \sim } 2 0$ min per field-of-view (FOV), it requires a high power laser $( \sim 2 5 ~ \mathrm { W } )$ and therefore does not reflect the typical Raman microscope setup.12 Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy, on the other hand, was first reported in 2008.13 15 SRS microscopy leverages the stimulated Raman gain and loss effect as the contrasting mechanism, which was first discovered serendipitously in 1962 by Woodbury and $\mathrm { N g . } ^ { 1 6 , 1 7 }$ This nonlinear optical process involves energy transfer between pump and Stokes beams and was initially used as a laser shifter (commonly known as Raman laser), $1 7 - 2 2$ later finding applications in time-resolved spectroscopy.27Other oable applications involve characterizing the Raman spectra of fluorescent molecules.

Notable innovations include video-rate imaging, single-molecule vibrational imaging, super-resolution SRS, hyperspectral SRS, and quantumenhanced SRS, among others.4159 Vibrational probes provide another wave of applications of metabolic imaging, supermultiplexed imaging, and vibrational sensing to address biological complexity.9,6072 Going beyond biomedical applications, SRS microscopy also finds broad impact on materials science, battery research, drug development, and environmental science.29,7377 
Despite its remarkable success, both the invention and the subsequent development of SRS microscopy are driven more empirically than rationally. A few careful reflections support this assessment. First, the notion of choosing SRS microscopy over its spontaneous counterpart is contrary to conventional wisdom. As single-molecule fluorescence spectroscopy and microscopy have transformed analytical chemistry and optical microscopy in the late 1990s, the chemistry community has long embraced the notion of background-free detection.7880 As a result, when it comes to sensitive detection of light emission, background-free spontaneous emission (i.e., fluorescence) is almost always favored over stimulated emission. Similarly, when it comes to light scattering, few would have conceptually predicted that SRS's sensitivity could surpass spontaneous Raman, which is theoretically background-free. Indeed, in addition to rate enhancements, SRS introduces additional laser intensity noise, unlike the "noise-free" nature of spontaneous Raman. Thus, enhanced "stimulated" rate in SRS does not necessarily translate to improved sensitivity, which explains why SRS was not regarded by spectroscopists for sensitive detection in most of the history. Second, as detailed in the original papers, the main motivation of developing SRS microscopy was to overcome the nonresonant background in coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy, another popular nonlinear Raman based chemical imaging technique at the time.13,28,81 Although SRS can indeed circumvent the inherent shortcomings faced by CARS,28 SRS was not proven to surpass the sensitivity of conventional spontaneous Raman in those original works. Third, in the subsequent 15 years or more, the SRS microscopy literature has always been using a proportionality relation to calculate the SRS signal.13,28,30,82, The lack of a definitive equation hinders quantitative understanding, leaving a number of key questions unanswered. For instance, is SRS microscopy a natural extension of SRS spectroscopy and why was SRS microscopy invented many decades later? Is SRS microscopy inherently more sensitive than spontaneous Raman microscopy? What are the origin, exact value, and physical significance of the "enhancement factor" cited in SRS studies? 

In this Perspective, we attempt to explicitly elucidate the fundamental principle of SRS microscopy. Our analysis here is built upon our recent quantum electrodynamics treatment. This framework established a Einstein-coefficient-like connection between the cross sections of stimulated and spontaneous Raman processes, revealed previously unknown duality of Raman scattering, and provided a formula to calculate the absolute SRS signal.84- 88 Here we continue this line of research and specifically analyze the ultimate Raman detection limits in the context of spatiotemporal resolutions. We unveil that spontaneous Raman scattering and stimulated Raman scattering occupy complementary territories with a boundary crossover line coinciding with biologically relevant scale. At low spatiotemporal resolution, SRS is actually less sensitive to spontaneous Raman, explaining why SRS spectroscopy (typically done with large volume and long time) does not bring higher sensitivity and why historically scientists did not regard SRS for sensitive detection. To the contrary, SRS excels in high spatiotemporal regimes, explaining the superior ability of SRS microscopy for chemical imaging at a small length scale and fast time scale. Therefore, instead of being a natural continuation of SRS spectroscopy, SRS emerges as a superb microscopy technique at refined spatiotemporal limits.

Abstract 
Label-free chemical contrast is highly desirable in biomedical imaging. Spontaneous Raman microscopy provides specific vibrational signatures of chemical bonds, but is often hindered by low sensitivity. Here we report a three-dimensional multiphoton vibrational imaging technique based on stimulated Raman scattering (SRS). The sensitivity of SRS imaging is significantly greater than that of spontaneous Raman microscopy, which is achieved by implementing highfrequency (megahertz) phase-sensitive detection. SRS microscopy has a major advantage over previous coherent Raman techniques in that it offers background-free and readily interpretable chemical contrast. We show a variety of biomedical applications, such as differentiating distributions of omega-3 fatty acids and saturated lipids in living cells, imaging of brain and skin tissues based on intrinsic lipid contrast, and monitoring drug delivery through the epidermis. 
Vibrational microscopies based on infrared absorption and Raman scattering $( 1 , 2 )$ have been used as label-free contrast mechanisms based on characteristic frequencies of various chemical bonds. However, infrared microscopy has limited spatial resolution because of long infrared wavelengths. Spontaneous Raman scattering microscopy, while having higher spatial resolution due to shorter excitation wavelengths, is insensitive and thus often has limited imaging speed. Coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy offers higher sensitivity than spontaneous Raman microscopy (3, 4). However, a CARS spectrum is different from its corresponding spontaneous Raman spectrum due to a nonresonant background, which complicates spectral assignment, causes difficulties in image interpretation, and limits detection sensitivity. 
Here we explore stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) as an imaging contrast mechanism. SRS is analogous (5, 6) to the well-known phenomenon of stimulated emission (7) and was first observed in 1962 (8). It has been used in many spectroscopic studies (9–12). In

Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy. An integrated laser (picoEMERALD with custom modification, Applied Physics and Electronics, Inc.) was used as a light source for both pump and Stokes beams. Briefly, picoEMERALD provided an output pulse train at $1 { , } 0 6 4 \mathrm { n m }$ with 6-ps pulse width and 80-MHz repetition rate, which served as the Stokes beam. The frequency-doubled beam at $5 3 2 \mathrm { n m }$ was used to synchronously seed a picosecond optical parametric oscillator (OPO) to produce a mode-locked pulse train (the idler beam of the OPO was blocked with an interferometric filter) with 5–6-ps pulse width. The wavelength of the OPO was tunable from $7 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ to $9 9 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , which served as the pump beam. The intensity of the $1 { , } 0 6 4 \mathrm { n m }$ Stokes beam was modulated sinusoidally by a built-in electro-optic modulator (EOM) at 8MHz with a modulation depth of more than $9 5 \%$ . The pump beam was spatially overlapped with the Stokes beam with a dichroic mirror inside picoEMERALD. The temporal overlap between pump and Stokes pulse trains was ensured with a built-in delay stage and optimized by the SRS signal of deuterium oxide $( 9 9 . 9 \mathrm { a t \% }$ D, 151882 ALDRICH). 
Pump and Stokes beams were coupled into an inverted laser-scanning microscope (FV1200MPE, Olympus) optimized for near-infrared throughput. A $2 5 \times$ water objective (XLPlan N, 1.05 numerical aperture (NA), MP, Olympus) with high near-infrared transmission and large field of view was used for measurements of all solutions, cells and tissues unless otherwise specified. A $6 0 \times$ water objective (UPlanAPO/IR, 1.2 NA, Olympus) with high near-infrared transmission was used for the X-gal assay and live-cell 8-colour imaging. The pump/Stokes beam size was matched to fill the back-aperture of the corresponding objectives for imaging. The forward-going pump and Stokes beams after passing through the samples were collected in transmission with a high-NA condenser lens (oil immersion, $1 . 4 \mathrm { N A }$ , Olympus), which was aligned following Köhler illumination. A telescope was then used to image the scanning mirrors onto a large-area $\mathrm { 1 0 m m \times 1 0 m m }$ ) Si photodiode (FDS1010, Thorlabs) to descan beam motion during laser scanning. The photodiode was reverse-biased by $6 4 \mathrm { V }$ from a DC power supply to increase the saturation threshold and the response bandwidth. A high-optical-density bandpass filter (890/220 CARS, Chroma Technology) was used to block the Stokes beam completely and transmit the pump beam only. The output current of the photodiode was electronically pre-filtered by an 8-MHz band-pass filter (KR 2724, KR electronics) to suppress the 80-MHz laser pulsing and the low-frequency contribution due to laser scanning across the scattering sample. It was then fed into a radio-frequency lock-in amplifier (SR844, Stanford Research Systems or HF2LI, Zurich instrument), terminated with $5 0 \Omega$ to demodulate the stimulated Raman loss signal experienced by the pump beam. The in-phase X-output of the lock-in amplifier was fed back into the analogue interface box (FV10-ANALOGUE) of the microscope. 
All laser powers were measured after the objective lens. For the spectroscopy measurement in Fig. 1, the Stokes laser power was $\begin{array} { r } { P _ { \mathrm { S t o k e s } } = 1 8 . 4 \mathrm { m W } . } \end{array}$ For the detection sensitivity measurement, pump and Stokes laser powers were $P _ { \mathrm { p u m p } } { = } 2 4 \mathrm { m W }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { P _ { \mathrm { S t o k e s } } = 1 8 4 \mathrm { m W } , } \end{array}$ respectively. SUMMARY 
Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) is a nonlinear Raman scattering process that can amplify Raman scattering by up to $1 0 ^ { 8 }$ times under modern microscopy configuration. SRS microscopy has emerged as a powerful chemical imaging technique due to its high chemical, spatial, and temporal resolution. While SRS microscopy was originally designed for biomedical applications, it has drawn increasingly more attention from the materials science community in recent years. The high-speed and high-chemical sensitivity of SRS are attractive for both high-throughput material characterizations and capturing transient dynamics in chemical transport and reactions. It has been explored in various topics, such as 2D materials, energy storage and conversion, and polymerizations with great success. In this review, we discuss principles, instrumentation, and current applications of SRS microscopy in materials science, followed by our perspectives on future exciting topics to be studied by SRS microscopy.

[Abstract] Abstract 
As a superb tool to visualize and study the spatial-temporal distribution of chemicals, Raman microscopy has made big impacts to many disciplines of science. While the label-free imaging has been the prevailing strategy in Raman microscopy, recent development and applications of vibrational/Raman tags, particularly when coupled with stimulated Raman Scattering (SRS) microscopy, have generated intense excitement in biomedical imaging. SRS imaging of vibrational tags has enabled researchers to study a wide range of small biomolecules with high specificity, sensitivity and multiplex capability, at single live cell level, tissue level or even in vivo. As reviewed in the article, this platform has facilitated imaging distribution and dynamics of small molecules such as glucose, lipids, amino acids, nucleic acids, and drugs that are otherwise difficult to do with other means. As both the vibrational tags and Raman instrumental development progress rapidly and synergistically, we anticipate that the technique will shed light onto an even broader spectrum of biomedical problems. 
Graphic abstract 
In this article, we review the recently successful applications of SRS and vibrational tags on biological problems.

d95ef40ebfb6_abstract: Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) describes a family of techniques first discovered and developed in the 1960s. Whereas the nascent history of the technique is parallel to that of laser light sources, recent advances have spurred a resurgence in its use and development that has spanned across scientific fields and spatial scales. SRS is a nonlinear technique that probes the same vibrational modes of molecules that are seen in spontaneous Raman scattering. While spontaneous Raman scattering is an incoherent technique, SRS is a coherent process, and this fact provides several advantages over conventional Raman techniques, among which are much stronger signals and the ability to time-resolve the vibrational motions. Technological improvements in pulse generation and detection strategies have allowed SRS to probe increasingly smaller volumes and shorter time scales. This has enabled SRS research to move from its original domain, of probing bulk media, to imaging biological tissues and single cells at the micro scale, and, ultimately, to characterizing samples with subdiffraction resolution at the nanoscale. Results 
Insect-derived PrAMPs apidaecin 1b and oncopeltus antimicrobial peptide have been optimized mostly in tryptic soy broth (TSB) providing promising lead structures Api88 and Api137 as well as Onc72, Onc110, and Onc112, respectively (Table 1, ESM Table S1) [3–6, 24]. Their interactions with bacterial targets, i.e., DnaK and 70S ribosome, have been commonly studied, whereas only a few publications addressed their cellular uptake in quantitative terms. However, the typically dye-labeled PrAMPs may not correctly reflect the uptake, cellular distribution, and degradation of free PrAMPs. Thus, we used RP-HPLC to quantify unlabeled PrAMPs in bacteria cultures. TSB medium showed a very high background even after TCA precipitation that works well for serum and cell lysates [3, 24], which prevented the sensitive detection of PrAMPs. More promising was the low background of Muller-Hinton broth (MHB), the standard medium for antibacterial activity assays according to CLSI standards, allowing quantification of all five studied PrAMPs at medium concentrations of $6 4 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / m L }$ . The MICs of Api88 and Api137 against $E$ . coli BL21AI were identical in TSB and MHB $( 2 \mu \mathrm { g } / \mathrm { m L } )$ and even 2-fold lower for all three oncocin analogs in MHB than in TSB (Table 1). 

Bacterial uptake of PrAMPs quantified by UVabsorbance 
RP-HPLC in combination with a UV detector to record the absorbance of PrAMPs at $2 1 4 ~ \mathrm { n m }$ was less sensitive than detection of fluorophore-labeled dyes requiring 100-fold higher cell numbers. Despite the unusually high cell densities, the antibacterial activities did not alter significantly for $E .$ . coli BL21AI, but decreased strongly for Api88, Api137, and Onc72 against E. coli BW25113 (ESM Table S2). 
The total PrAMP quantities determined in cell pellet, medium, and wash fractions of each cell culture provided high recovery rates ranging from $7 5 \%$ (Onc112) to $9 5 \%$ (Onc110), indicating that most of the initially added peptide amounts were detectable (ESM Fig. S2A). This confirmed a valid quantification of Api137, Onc110, and Onc112 in all three fractions of the uptake study. The recovery rates decreased during incubation, especially for Api88 and Onc72 with only 25 and $2 9 \%$ intact peptide detected after $^ { 1 \mathrm { h } }$ , respectively. The decreasing recovery rates correlated well to the different halflife times determined for all five peptides in mouse serum and bacterial lysates, where Api88 and Onc72 are much less stable than Api137, Onc110, and Onc112 [5, 24]. Indeed, degradation in the cell culture was confirmed by metabolites known from previous stability studies. When the quantities of the major metabolites, i.e., Api88(1–17), Onc72(1–14), and Onc72(1–16), were considered in addition to Api88 and Onc72, the recovery rates increased to 67 and $49 \%$ , respectively, after an incubation period of $^ { 1 \mathrm { h } }$ . Besides these metabolites, MALDI mass spectra recorded on a Q-TOF Synapt 
G2Si MS (Waters, MS Technologies, Manchester, UK) for further chromatographic fractions representing small peak areas revealed further metabolites with molecular weights of 2091.27 and 2291.39 Da in Onc72 and Api88 samples, respectively, which might correspond to Onc72(3–19) (monoisotopic mass $2 0 9 1 . 2 4 ~ \mathrm { D a } )$ and C-terminally deamidated Api88 (monoisotopic mass $2 2 9 1 . 3 4 ~ \mathrm { D a } )$ ), although the structures could not be confirmed by tandem mass spectrometry.

These peptide quantities remained stable for Api137 for the next $3 0 ~ \mathrm { m i n }$ , but decreased for the other peptides, especially for Api88 to only $8 . 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { g } \left( 1 3 \% \right)$ . 
Analysis of low peptide amounts by LC-MS/MS 
The moderate sensitivity of the RP-HPLC approach did not allow reducing the peptide amounts further in the uptake assays. Thus, we applied RP-HPLC-ESI-MS/MS using MRM, as recently reported for Api88, Api137, Onc72, and Onc112 providing limits of quantification (LOQ) of 15, 30, 53, and $4 6 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / L }$ , respectively, in the absence of biological matrix [8, 9]. After optimization in the presence of sample matrix ( $E .$ . coli supernatant, $2 5 \%$ MHB), the LOQs were 25, 135, 25, and $2 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / L }$ , respectively (ESM Fig. S1). This allowed a further reduction of the peptide concentrations in the uptake studies to the MIC values determined for low and surprisingly also for high cell numbers of $E$ . coli BL21AI (Table 1 and ESM Table S2). 

When $E$ . coli BL21AI cultures were incubated with apidaecin $2 \mu \mathrm { g } / \mathrm { m L } )$ and oncocin analogs $( 4 \mu \mathrm { g / m L } )$ ), the peptides entered the cells again rapidly. Already at the first time point ( $\mathrm { { 0 } \ m i n } ,$ ), high peptide quantities of 0.8 to $1 . 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { g }$ were detected in the pellets of cells treated with Onc112 $2 8 \%$ of total peptide amount added), Onc110 $( 2 0 \% )$ , and Api137 $(40 \% )$ , while Api88 ( $0 . 4 ~ \mu \mathrm { g }$ , $20 \%$ ) and Onc72 $( 0 . 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { g }$ , $7 . 5 \% )$ were present at 2-fold lower quantities (Fig. 1b, ESM Fig. S2B). The low uptake of Onc72 can be explained again by its intracellular proteolytic degradation (ESM Fig. S2B). This was confirmed by the even decreasing Onc72 quantities at the later time points, which was also observed for Api88. Surprisingly, the content of Api137 decreased already at $3 0 ~ \mathrm { m i n }$ and even further to $0 . 4 ~ { \mu \mathrm { g } }$ after $6 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ , although metabolites were not detected. 
Interestingly, 20 to $30 \%$ of the peptides were detected in the wash fraction at $0 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ , but significantly less at later time points. This indicates that the peptides interact very fast with the outer bacterial membrane or reversibly penetrate into the periplasm, where they can still be washed out. This is in agreement with the previous experiment using a high peptide concentration $( 6 4 \mu \mathrm { g / m L } )$ ), although the relative peptide contents were lower (2.0 to $8 . 6 \%$ ) demonstrating that the cell surface and maybe the periplasm were saturated by PrAMPs added at such high concentrations (ESM Fig. S2). All PrAMPs including apidaecin and oncocin analogs studied so far appear to rely mostly on the SbmA transporter, whereas only a few PrAMPs like Onc112 can additionally enter $E$ . coli via the yjiL-mdtM gene cluster [15, 16]. In MHB, all oncocin analogs were inactive against $E$ . coli BW25113 ΔsbmA yjiL::Tn10, and the activities of Api88 and Api137 decreased further 4-fold and 8-fold, respectively. 
As MHB did not affect the quantification by LC-MS, the uptake was studied by incubating $E .$ coli BL21AI with Api88 and Onc72 at a concentration of $6 4 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / m L }$ . The initial pellet amounts were 7.0 and $1 . 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / m L }$ , respectively, which increased to 19.5 and $3 . 4 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / m L }$ , respectively, after $3 0 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ and decreased afterwards to around the initial values (ESM Fig. S3A). Thus, the selectivity of LC-MS provides more accurate quantification when analyzing AMPs in medium. In contrast, the recoveries of metabolites Api88(1–16) and Api88(1–17) were higher by RP-HPLC.

1. Introduction 
As we know, noble metal nanoparticles (NPs) have special optical properties and are widely applied in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology and life science.1–8 As a powerful optical functional material, the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) of the noble metal NPs are closely related to their structural parameters, including size, shape, composition, and morphology.9–11 Thus, the controllable synthesis of noble metal NPs is a very interesting topic and much effort has been devoted to develop the available methods to create metal nanostructures, such as the hydrothermal method, the galvanic replacement method, the oil/water interface method and the template method.12–15 It is an essential that noble metal NPs with special structures are prepared to manipulate fully their distinctive LSPR properties. In particular, great study has been directed to the design of novel hollow noble metal nanostructures due to their high active surface-to-volume ratio and fascinating applications in numerous areas of optoelectronic imaging, catalysis, environmental monitoring, biosensing, diagnosis and drug delivery.16–20 

On the other hand, surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) has attracted a great deal of attention because the Raman signal can usually be enhanced by several orders of magnitude for target molecules attached on noble metal surfaces.21,22 The generation mechanism of SERS is widely recognized as involving two major components: chemical and electromagnetic enhancement. The former component is due to an increased polarizability of the target molecules under the influence of incident radiation, as a result of which new chemical bands with the metal surface are formed.23,24 The latter component arises from the enhancement of the electromagnetic field for the occurrence of the LSPR of the nanostructured noble metal systems and is highly dependent on matching between the excitation wavelength and the LSPR band.25,26 As a non-destructive and ultrasensitive spectroscopy analysis technique SERS, originating from electromagnetic enhancement, is more suitable for the detection of biological tissues by using incident radiation in the ‘‘window of optical transparency’’, i.e., in the near infrared (NIR) spectral region of $7 5 0 \mathrm { - } 1 0 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m }$ .27,28 Consequence, the LSPR band of the noble metal nanostructures in such an NIR region possesses obvious superiority and promising applications for biomedical detection. 

With regard to the window of optical transparency, we hope that the structure of noble metal NPs can be tailored to satisfy the requirement of its LSPR band close to the wavelength of incident radiation in the NIR region. For example, the LSPR bands of solid spherical gold NPs (GNPs) can be tuned by as much as $5 0 \ \mathrm { n m }$ around $5 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , and the bands of hollow NPs can be continuously adjusted from 500 to $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ by controlling the size of the interior hollows.29–32 Furthermore, the noble metal nanostructures with rough surfaces have a relatively high SERS intensity because of the existence of ‘‘hot spots’’ (strongly enhanced electromagnetic areas) on the junctions and sharp tips of nanostructures,33–35 so that great efforts have been directed towards the fabrication of noble metal NPs with various morphologies including raspberries,36 flowers,37 meatballs,38 stars,39 and sea urchins.40,41 Thus, a hollow metal nanostructure with a rough morphology is naturally considered to combine their merits, that is, the adjustability of the LSPR band and the high SERS intensity. However, it is a complex chemical process to synthesize a hollow metal nanostructure with rough morphology. Generally, silver seeds should be first be synthesized to build a hollow center in the GNPs,42 and then the rough morphology of the hollow GNPs are produced by using organic molecules as the capping agent, or stabilizers such as cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB),15,43 gum arabic,38 sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS),44 and gelatin protein.45 A typical sacrificial template approach and the galvanic replacement reaction between Ag NPs and $\mathrm { \ H A u C l _ { 4 } }$ have been introduced to form hollow GNPs with an urchin-like shell by the aid of ascorbic acid as reducer and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) as dispersant.46 The introduction of these organic molecules will block the linking of the target molecules to the surface of the GNPs, which inevitably impairs the following SERS applications. Therefore, it is still an enormous challenge to achieve the finely tailored structure of hollow GNPs with sophisticated morphology by a green and simple synthesize process. 
In this article, we demonstrate a facile and environmentally friendly galvanic replacement strategy for high-yield synthesis of hollow sea urchin gold nanoparticles (HSU-GNPs). Introduction 
Surface plasmon based surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS)1 is a leading non-destructive technique that helps to extend the sensitivity of Raman spectroscopy to the level of a single molecule.2,3 Generally, the strongly enhanced local neareld originating from the surface plasmon resonance (SPR) effect on the metal nanostructures is the main mechanism for surface plasmon based SERS.4 In recent years, a large local neareld enhancement generated from the local surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) effect in a specic region around or its intercoupling effect between metal NPs, which is dened as a ‘hot spot’, has drawn researchers' attention and been widely proposed and demonstrated for single molecule level detection.5–7 Due to the special geometries with controllable morphologies and parameters,8–10 adjustable plasmon bands9,10 and resonance modes11–15 can be easily realized in metal hollow nano-structures. Thus, they have been extensively studied and applied to highly sensitive SERS sensing given the highly localized near-eld7,15 and the corresponding regular hot spots around the nanoparticles.16–19 M. A. Mahmoud and his coworkers have symmetrically investigated both the surface plasmon resonance and the coupling properties of gold hollow nanocages by optimizing the size and shell thickness aiming for highly sensitive SERS detection.18 

Multipole SPR modes on gold or silver nanostructures, such as core shells,7,8,20 nanoprisms,21 nanorods22,23 or spherical particles,24,25 have been observed in previous studies. Recently, these multipole plasmonic resonance modes in metal shells or cavity structures have gained much renewed attention due to the potential applications in bio-sensing,26 uorescence,27 nanolasers,28,29 or nonlinear nano-photonics.30 Commonly, a highly localized electromagnetic eld can be obtained in or on the plasmonic cavities through the resonances in multipole modes, which have been proposed to create high quality (Q) factor plasmonic resonators31,32 or ultra-small-mode-volume devices, e.g. nanolasers, surface plasmon amplication by stimulated emission of radiation (SPASER), etc.28,29 Additionally, by using the highly localized electromagnetic elds on the exterior surface of a plasmonic resonator, in which plasmonic whispering-gallery mode (WGM) resonance happens, the cavity can be potentially used as a WGM resonator based bio-sensor with a high sensitivity of up to $5 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m }$ per refraction index unit, and wide detection range.26 
Here, in this work, multipole plasmon resonances were realized in the self-assembled Ag hollow-nanospheres (HNSs). 
Beneting from higher order plasmonic resonances, a highly localized near-eld around the surface and hot spots generated by the inter-coupling effect in the gaps were obtained within the HNS arrays, which were then demonstrated to be an ideal SERS substrate by taking advantage of these enhanced local elds. The large scale two-dimensional (2D) Ag HNS arrays were fabricated using the self-assembled polystyrene (PS) nanospheres as the template with its size and gaps adjusted by employing reactive-ion etching (RIE) on the template. Dipole, quadrupole, octupole and hexadecapole mode plasmonic resonances are distinguishably resolved from the extinction spectra showing good agreement with the simulated spectra and neareld distributions. According to the FDTD simulation results, highly localized electromagnetic eld distribution and strong regular hot spots were obtained around or in the gaps between the Ag HNSs through the interparticle coupling effect, which are believed to be responsible for the highly sensitive SERS performance on the Ag HNS arrays with the optimized size and gaps. Further Raman mapping from this metal hollow structure evidences these periodic plasmonic cavity arrays to be a stable and uniform SERS-active substrate.

[Conclusion] CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES 
Hollow gold nanostructures have drawn attention for their biomedical applications because of their unique physical and optical properties, such as facile LSPR tunability, drug loading capacity, and enhanced photothermal activity, compared to those of conventional solid gold nanoparticles. In this review, we summarized the recent research trends in hollow gold nanostructures, including synthetic methods, physical/optical characteristics, and recent advances in biomedical applications. Various forms of hollow gold nanostructures can be synthesized by either hard- or soft-templating methods, but the majority of synthesis is based on galvanic replacement. While the LSPR peaks of solid gold nanoparticles depend solely on the overall size of the particles, those of hollow gold nanostructures are greatly influenced not only by the size, but also by the thickness of the shell. Therefore, the LSPR peaks can be easily adjusted while maintaining the overall size of the particles, which provides additional tunability of the SERS signal or photothermal activity. The voids in the interior also provide additional functionality to hollow gold nanostructures by being utilized as nanoscale storage for impregnating functional materials (e.g., anticancer drugs), which is not possible in solid gold nanoparticles. Based on these characteristics, various hollow gold nanostructures have been widely used in several biomedical applications, including biosensors, photothermal therapy, and biomedical imaging. It should be noted that there have been many studies aimed at the synergistic effects of simultaneously utilizing the various functionalities of hollow gold nanostructures, such as combined chemo–photothermal therapy, light-responsive drug release, and plasmonic nanostructure-based bioimaging. Despite this progress, there are still many issues: 1) off- and on-target accumulation of hollow gold nanostructures and 2) preventing the aggregation and disassembly of hollow gold nanostructures. Large-sized hollow gold nanostructures (larger than $2 0 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ can lead undesirable accumulation in the reticuloendothelial system (e.g., liver, spleen, and lungs); on the other hand, very small-sized one cannot provide sufficient on-target accumulation of them due to the short circulation time. Even if the size of these structures is suitable for selective accumulation, the aggregation and disassembly of hollow gold nanostructures in human body can decrease the LSPR intensity.

$1 0 6 4 \mathrm { n m }$ SERS detection of NIR active hollow gold nanotags has been demonstrated. Red-shifted HGNs are small (below $1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ ) and spherical in shape which means they have the potential to penetrate cellular membranes and tissue cells easily. They are less toxic to cells than silica coated and solid gold nanoparticles42 and are stable in sodium citrate allowing for easier functionalisation of the outer shells. Because of the high sensitivity, molecular specificity, and non-invasive sampling technique, surface enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) is one of the most powerful analytical techniques. Additionally, its low interference from water makes SERS uniquely effective for the biological sensing. In the last decade, the emergence of life-threatening pathogens and debilitating diseases has outpaced the development of treatments. As a result, detection and monitoring have become the first guard approach to containing the spread of deadly infections such as Ebola, H1N1, and most recently SARS-CoV-2. As a result, recent SERS research has heavily focused on the study of biological processes and point of care diagnostics. Raman spectroscopy is a vibrational spectroscopy of ability to detect chemical bonds via photon scattering, but the generated signals are extremely weak comparing to the incident beam. Thus, surface enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) is introduced to overcome such inherent limitation and interrogate trace materials by exploiting the enormous electromagnetic field enhancement resulted from the excitation of localized surface plasmon resonances at nanostructured metallic surfaces, mostly gold or silver26, 27 . It has been widely applied for biological analysis, e.g., living cell classification28 , cancer detection29, biological imaging30 and virus detection31 . For SARS-CoV-2, the spike glycoprotein consists of S1 and S2 subunits, and S1 subunit contains a receptor binding domain (RBD) directly recognizing the human receptor angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) for cell entry 32, 33 . Such recognition and binding might alter the structure of ACE2 and lead to changes in Raman spectra. Additionally, the binding specificity allows ACE2 as an anchor to capture SARS-CoV-2 from human or environmental specimens for interrogation.

1. Introduction 
The COvID-19 pandemic has impacted the world way of living in an unprecedented manner, since its discovery in Wuhan (China) by the end of 2019. More than a year later (the time of writing this manuscript), the numbers of infected and dead people is still increasing by the widespread of the virus [1,2]. The SARS-CoV-2 virus fits them with corona virus family having single stranded genetic material RNA and surface proteins like membrane (M), envelope (E), nucleocapsid (N) and spike (S). S protein is of particulate interest since, it serves as mediator to the host cells via ACE-2 enzymes (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2). It is categorized as largest surface protein virus being 180kDa spike monomer which makes its vitality to attach to the human host cells faster. The Spike trimers were the core component that invades the host cells with 

ACE-2. The remarkable feature of the SARS-CoV-2 virus is its higher mutability and fast transmission rates which could pose great challenges to detect as well as cure the infections [3,4]. To ease the situation, Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and Real-time reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) standalone as foremost diagnostic tools which involves the extraction of RNA to confirm the positive cases which takes almost more than $^ { 5 - 6 \mathrm { h } }$ [5,6]. On the other hand, ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays) makes use of IgM and IgG antibodies found to increase with patients is also an over-time consuming process [7]. Therefore, for the universal healthcare emergency, the development of detection techniques that are ultra-fast, reliable, inexpensive, and acknowledgeable by medical world represents an unmet need. 
Among several sophisticated analytical instruments, surfaceenhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) has proved its effectiveness in terms of unswerving, extreme sensitivity as well as high selectivity for identification of analytes under examination [810]. The technique has progressively evolved from the basic detection of chemical finger-print of organic molecules towards an alternative bio-analytical tool for the detection of microbes to a greater extent with excellent specificity and reproducibility by tailoring the design of substrates [1113]. Rapid trace level detection of micro-biological organisms with SERS will ease the spread of their diverse effects on human civilization. SERS emerged to be sensitive technique as well as ultra-fast in their detection mechanism. RT-PCR (based on nucleic acids) rely on particular time frame for evaluating the infections as positive (early stage of infection ie., 6 days before to 14 days after the symptom onset) leading some chances for false negatives at some cases which are not limited into this time frame of infectivity. The time duration for acquiring results is almost $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 8 h }$ . Whereas, SERS do not have the limit (at any stage of infection) to detect and able to get the results within $5 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ Besides for RNA extraction, specific reagents are needed to perform it which improves the cost for analysis (typically 100-300USD). In case of SERS, no need for the employment of reagents, direct detection is possible without raising the cost of analysis (typically 10-50usD) [14,15]. On comparison with RT-PCR, it is highly surface sensitive, hence the protein moieties of the SARS-CoV-2 virus could be detected deliberately. The variants reported with the subjects occurred with the mutant changes in the copies of genetic code (i.e., nucleic acids), hence the discussed surface sensitive fails to detect the type of mutant variants via direct detection. Rather, false negative/ positive cases can be filed with the currently developed diagnostic tool based on the viral proteins. Hence it can standalone as a fast-screening tool to meet the demand of pandemic outbreak [14]. 

SERS principle discriminates the electromagnetic and chemical phenomena that ground when the analyte is adsorbed on the sensor' surface [16,17]. 1. Introduction 
The spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARs-CoV-2) has had a huge political, social, and cultural impact (He et al., 2020; Ferriti et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2019). Several different types of vaccines have been developed and distributed to control the spread to some extent; however, the world is suffering again due to the recent spread of mutations of the virus (Harvey et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a, b). As the number of confirmed cases of SARS-CoV-2 increases, it is essential to identify and isolate infected persons quickly. The reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) is currently used as a standard diagnostic method for SARS-CoV-2 (Smyrlaki et al., 2020). However, more rapid diagnostic technology is required to effectively respond to the virus's rapid spread since the RT-PCR method takes approximately $^ { 3 - 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ of diagnosis time, including viral RNA extraction, reverse transcription, thermocycling amplification, and fluorescence detection (Broughton et al. 2020; Long et al., 2020). An infection can be confirmed within $3 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ of using an immunochromatographic rapid kit that relies on an antibodyantigen reaction. However, the diagnostic sensitivity for a recently infected or asymptomatic infected person is remarkably low $5 0 \%$ or less) (Vandenberg et al., 2021; Corman et al., 2021). Thus, there is a problem with the reliability of the diagnosis. In particular, the issue of "false-negative" results, whereby positive patients are diagnosed as negative, is the main reason this method cannot be adopted as a standard diagnostic method (Ghodake et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2020). Therefore, many researchers are striving to develop a new molecular diagnostic technology that can shorten the diagnostic time while maintaining the diagnostic accuracy of RT-PCR. 

Fluorescence detection using TaqMan probes is part of the RT-PCR process, but a gene amplification process involving 3040 thermocycles is essential because the detection sensitivity is limited (Hwang et al., 2021; Faulds et al., 2004). It would be possible to shorten the diagnosis time by reducing the number of thermocycling steps and using a more sensitive method than fluorescence detection. Recently, many studies have addressed the use of the surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERs) detection method, which offers a better detection sensitivity than fluorescence detection (Sitjar et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a, b; Zhang et al., 2021; Ramos-Guzman et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). If a biomarker molecule related to the change in the concentration of the target genes can exist in a nanogap, the localized surface plasmon resonance effect would greatly amplify any incident light (Baumberg et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017). We recently reported on a novel nano-plasmonic detection platform that produces high-sensitivity SERS signals with regularly arranged gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) in the cavities of Au nanodimple substrates (AuNDSs) (Dang et al., 2021). The AuNPs were uniformly arranged over the AuNDS cavity surface by DNA hybridization. Thus, it is possible to attain a high level of sensitivity using strongly enhanced SERS signals for the specific gene markers generated in this nanogap. 

In this study, we developed a new SERS-based SARS-CoV-2 diagnostic platform using previously reported AuNP-internalized AuNDS (Dang et al., 2021). This method can dramatically reduce the diagnostic time relative to conventional RT-PCR, which is currently used as a standard diagnostic method for SARS-CoV-2. The assay results for the envelope protein (E) and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) genes of SARS-CoV-2 were compared with those measured by RT-PCR and magnetic bead-based SERS-PCR. The AuNDS-based SERS-PCR system addressed in this work could detect bridge DNAs with fewer than ten thermocycling steps; therefore, it can dramatically reduce the diagnosis time relative to the currently used RT-PCR. Furthermore, we propose a SERS-PCR system that integrates a sampling module capable of automatically assaying samples and AuNPs into AuNDS with a portable Raman spectrophotometer, that is, a next-generation molecular diagnostic system capable of contributing to the rapid and accurate diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2.
