Comparison of the Raman spectra obtained from free Tyr, Gly–Tyr– Gly, and lysozyme (Fig. 1) permits identification of seven common Raman markers located at ${ \sim } 1 6 1 6 \ c m ^ { - 1 }$ (Y1), ${ \sim } 1 6 0 8 \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ (Y2), $\sim 1 2 1 0 \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ (Y3), ${ \sim } 1 1 7 8 \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ (Y4), ${ \sim } 8 5 0 \ c m ^ { - 1 }$ (Y5), ${ \sim } 8 3 0 \ c m ^ { - 1 }$ (Y6), and ${ \sim } 6 4 3 \ c m ^ { - 1 }$ (Y7), which can be assigned to Tyr. Among these modes, Y1 and Y2 markers are both located at the low wavenumber limit of the so-called amide I region. In contrast, none of them can perturb the peptide chain structural analysis through the amide III markers $( 1 3 2 0 - 1 2 2 0 mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ ). In the case of Gly–Tyr– Gly, some subtle differences could be revealed with a recently reported spectrum,[24] which can be all attributed to the ${ \mathsf { C } } ^ { \mathsf { t e r } }$ amide group of the presently used tripeptide. 

Because of the low solubility of free Tyr in aqueous solution (vide supra), the influence of the environmental parameters, such as concentration, temperature, pH, and isotopic substitution, was preferentially analyzed on Gly–Tyr–Gly, because of the following: (1) The observed Raman intensity of this compound is dominated by that arising from its central Tyr residue (Fig. 1), and (2) the Raman spectra obtained by increasing either the peptide concentration $( 2 . 5 { - } 2 0 \mathsf { m M } )$ (Fig. S1) or the solution temperature $( 5 - 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C } )$ 
(Fig. S2) do not manifest a perceptible perturbation on the characteristic Tyr markers. This fact leads us to presume that in this compound, the auto-association favored particularly by $\pi - \pi$ interactions of phenol rings should be rather negligible. 
Upon increasing pH to extremely basic values, drastic changes appear in different Raman bands (Fig. 2, top), for instance, (1) the apparition of a medium intensity band at $1 6 6 1 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ , consistent with the $N H _ { 3 } ^ { + }  N H _ { 2 }$ conversion at the $\mathsf { N } ^ { \mathsf { t e r } }$ side of the tripeptide; (2) the large downshift $1 6 1 6 \to 1 6 0 1 ( \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 } )$ of Y1, accompanied by a 2.5-fold increase of its relative intensity; (3) the complete vanishing of Y2 (at ${ \sim } 1 6 0 8 \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ ; and (4) the considerable intensity decrease $( \sim 5 0 \% )$ of Y4, with a slight downshift of its wavenumber $( 1 1 7 8 \to 1 1 7 4 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ ). Furthermore, the intensity ratio of the doublet at ${ \sim } 8 5 0 / 8 3 0 \ c m ^ { - 1 }$ (Y5/Y6) tends toward unity at high $\mathsf { p H } ,$ with a slight downshift of its lower wavenumber component (Y6). The changes observed in the characteristic Tyr Raman markers upon increasing pH corroborate those reported recently in an octapeptide.[20] 

Figure 2 (bottom) reveals the effect of $\mathsf { H } \to \mathsf { D }$ isotopic substitution (1) in the backbone $\mathsf { N H } _ { 3 } ^ { + } \ ( \mathsf { N } ^ { \mathsf { t e r } } )$ and ${ \mathsf { N H } } _ { 2 }$ $( C ^ { \mathsf { t e r } } )$ end groups through the changes appearing in the medium bands above $1 6 3 0 \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ and (2) in the phenol ring OH group through a ${ \sim } 1 0 { \cdot } \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ wavenumber downshift and a ${ \sim } 8 0 \%$ loss of the relative intensity of Y2 marker. The intensity ratio of the Y5/Y6 doublet tends again toward unity, accompanied by a slight wavenumber downshift of its both components. 

Calculated structural and vibrational data 
For the sake of brevity, we have only reported in the main text the final theoretical data. All details were placed in Supporting Information. Relative energies and main geometrical parameters of the 27 optimized $T y r ( 0 ) + \mathsf { n } \mathsf { H } _ { 2 } O$ clusters, with $n = 5 , 6 ,$ and 7, are given in Table S1. Full graphical representation of these clusters was displayed in Figs S3, S5, and S7. It is worth mentioning that whatever the hydration number $( n )$ , the gauche- /gauche- orientation with respect to the side chain $( \chi _ { 1 } , \chi _ { 2 } )$ torsion angles dominates. In contrast, the backbone $( \varphi , \psi )$ torsion angles reveal a large variation, allowing stabilization of water molecules around the backbone $\mathsf { C O O } ^ { - }$ and $N H _ { 3 } ^ { + }$ groups. Theoretical Raman spectra obtained from T $\mathsf { y r } ( 0 ) + \mathsf { n } \mathsf { H } _ { 2 } \mathsf { O }$ clusters corresponding to $n = 5 - 7$ are shown in Figs S4, S6, and S8, respectively. Because of their high statistical weights, only those clusters with a relative energy (ΔE) not larger than ${ \sim } 1 . 2 \mathsf { k c a l m o l } ^ { - 1 }$ can significantly contribute to the final calculated spectrum at room temperature.[11,41] The thermal average of the calculated Raman spectra obtained from the different 

$T y r ( 0 ) + \mathsf { n } \mathsf { H } _ { 2 } 0$ clusters $( n = 5 - 7 )$ is displayed in Fig. 3 (traces A, B, and C) and compared with the observed Raman spectrum of Tyr at pH 7 (trace D). It can be concluded as follows: (1) Regardless the hydration number (n), all calculated Raman spectra account for the seven Tyr markers $( Y _ { i } , i = 1 , . . . , 7 )$ , and (2) the theoretical wavenumbers reproduce well the observed ones in the whole analyzed spectral region with a $\nu _ { \mathrm { o b s } } / \nu _ { \mathrm { c a l c } }$ ratio (where $\nu$ is the peak wavenumber) exceeding 0.97. This clearly justifies our choice not to apply any scaling factor to the theoretical wavenumbers; (3) as Table S2 shows, six out of the seven Tyr markers originate from the in-plane vibrations, except Y6 (the lower component of the Tyr doublet), which is clearly assigned to $\mathsf { C } \mathrm { - H }$ out-of-plane bending (wagging) motions. In a similar manner, the structural and vibrational features of tyrosinate were estimated by means of the deprotonated free Tyr, referred to as Tyr(-2) (Scheme 1). Table S2 reports the energetic and geometrical data of the four most stable clusters of Tyr(-2) $+ 7 H _ { 2 } O$ . Figure S9 displays their graphical representation, as well as their Raman spectra. Without going into details, the thermal average of the calculated Raman spectrum, referred to as ‘Sum’, satisfactorily reproduces the characteristic Raman markers of the deprotonated phenol ring detailed in the preceding section (Fig. 2, top). The assignment of the main peaks of the calculated Raman spectrum is reported in Table S2. Cartesian coordinates of the lowest-energy clusters of $T y r ( 0 ) + 7 H _ { 2 } O$ and $T y r ( - 2 ) + 7 H _ { 2 } O$ are provided in Table S3. 
Focus on Tyr doublet (Y5/Y6) 
Earliest interpretation based on $p$ -cresol 
This doublet is presumably one of the most documented aromatic fingerprints observed in the Raman spectra of peptides and proteins. Its components present a quite limited wavenumber variation $( \sim \pm 5 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 } )$ around their average values at 850 and $8 3 0  c m ^ { - 1 }$ (Fig. 1). The first interpretation of the Tyr doublet was suggested in 1975 by the pioneering work of Siamwiza et $a / . ^ { [ 1 2 ] }$ Briefly, the observations made on the para-substituted phenol ring containing simple compounds, such as $p$ -cresol (Scheme 1), have led the authors to the conclusion that only the higher wavenumber component of the Raman doublet (Y5, also called ring-breathing mode) can be assigned to a ring fundamental mode. Thus, the assignment of the lower wavenumber component (Y6) gave grounds for further reflection. An artful description of the doublet, as displayed in Scheme 2, was suggested based on a Fermi resonance effect between Y5 and the first overtone of another phenol ring out-of-plane mode located at $\sim 4 1 3 c m ^ { - 1 }$ . Even, more recent DFT calculations performed on $p$ -cresol[27] confirmed the earliest interpretation of the doublet,[12,13] because Y5 was the only component of the doublet, which could be interpreted by the calculated Raman spectrum obtained from this model compound. 

$p$ -cresol versus Tyr 
As already mentioned, the presently reported calculated Raman spectra (Fig. 3A–C) account for the seven Tyr markers by means of the phenol ring fundamental vibrations. Thus, there is no need to consider a Fermi resonance effect for interpreting the Tyr Y5/Y6 doublet. As a consequence, the question raised here is related to the exact reason behind the striking difference encountered between the theoretical data offered by $p$ -cresol and Tyr. Figure 4, at a glance, allows us to find out that this difference is purely due to the symmetrical features of these compounds. In fact, the lowest-energy conformer of $p$ -cresol presents a symmetrical character with respect to the phenol ring plane, because of the in-plane location of OH and the methyl group particular orientation. As a consequence, Y5 (in-plane mode) becomes Raman active, and Y6 (out-of-plane mode) Infrared (IR) active. Hence, Y6 cannot appear in the calculated Raman spectrum of $p$ -cresol. However, it should be noted that at normal and higher temperatures, the rotation of the methyl group, passing by low-energy barriers, can lead to a partial breakdown of the $p$ -cresol symmetry, rendering active Y6 in Raman spectra (but with a much lower intensity compared with Y5). This fact has been previously reported by Arp et al.[27] in the Raman spectra of $p$ -cresol liquid and vapor, where Y6 has been observed with a much lower intensity compared with Y5. Oppositely, the presence of the side chain in Tyr (instead of a methyl group) definitely lowers the global symmetry of the phenol ring. As a consequence, Y5 and Y6 become both 
Raman active, and the calculated Raman spectrum can naturally interpret the Y5/Y6 doublet. In other words, the inability of $p$ -cresol to account for the doublet is simply due to the inherent insufficiencies of this simple model compound for representing the structural and vibrational complexities of Tyr (or tyrosinate).

6.1. Selection of Raman Reporter Molecules 
The main requirements of an ideal Raman reporter molecule are as follows: (1) The reporter molecules must have a relatively large Raman scattering cross section to produce strong SERS signals. The optimal scenario involves an optical absorption of the Raman reporter that matches the excitation laser as well as the LSPR of the nanostructure, leading to an extra $1 0 ^ { 2 } { - } 1 0 ^ { 3 }$ enhancement due to the surface-enhanced resonance Raman scattering. For example, Graham et al. reported one of the first comprehensive studies of SERRS for DNA analysis with R6G labeled probes.213 Their results showed a sensitivity comparable to fluorescence microscopy which illustrated the importance of reporter molecules selection. (2) Raman reporter molecules should have a strong affinity for the metal surface to avoid the desorption during further modification or replacement by biomolecules in the detection environment. For example, Copper found that the signals from physisorbed labels including R6G, nile blue, crystal violet, and methylene blue decreased with increasing incubation time in the culture medium and cells due to the detachment of reporter molecules from the metal surface over time. However, chemisorbed labels provided stable signals inside cells for over $2 4 \mathrm { h }$ .103 (3) The molecules with characteristic and well-assigned Raman peaks could be helpful to avoid signal overlapping during multiplex detection. Traditional Raman reporters and biomolecules both present multiple Raman peaks in the fingerprint region, which may overlap with each other and are difficult to separate. Several chemical groups have been developed as Raman tags including alkyne, azide, nitrile, deuterium, and metal−carbonyl possessing characteristic peaks in the Raman silent region $( 2 0 0 0 { - } 2 7 0 0 \cdots ^ { - 1 }$ range). Olivo et al. designed a metal carbonyl based SERS tag by combining osmium carbonyl clusters with Au nanoparticles and used the enhanced CO signal at $2 0 3 0 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ to perform high-contrast live-cell imaging.220 Tan et al. used diphenylacetylene functionalized PEG as a Raman reporter which showed a characteristic peak around $2 0 3 0 ~ \mathrm { c m ^ { - 1 } }$ and obtained high-resolution Raman images of cells.221 Recently, Liu et al. prepared prussian blue coated Au nanoparticles as background-free SERS tags, as shown in Figure 23a. Prussian blue presents a strong and sharp single vibrational peak at $2 1 5 6 ~ \mathrm { c m ^ { - 1 } }$ and, more impressively, produces surfaceenhanced resonant Raman scattering in the visible light range.222 4-Mercaptobenzonitrile was also embedded in a core−shell nanostructure, which depicted a sharp Raman peak around 2232 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , to further enhance the SERS signal of Raman tags and achieve cell imaging with a high signal-to-background ratio in the following work.223 All these tags possessed the capacity to avoid overlapping with the peaks from the intracellular species and provided a very clear and high-contrast image of cells, especially when the concentration of target is low in the biosystems. 

However, compared with fluorescence microscopy, single component analysis by SERS is not advantageous. Since the bandwidth of SERS peaks is much narrower than that of fluorescence, SERS-based detection using functionalized nanotags possesses the capacity of multiplex detection with singlewavelength excitation. The multiplexed sensing ability is of great importance to a comprehensive understanding of the cell processes, monitoring of cell events, as well as accurate diagnosis of disease. For an efficient SERS-based multiplex detection, Raman tags must possess high stability when integrated into a system and well separated distinguishable peaks. Moreover, probes must be targeted with precision without cross interference to ensure that detected signals come from the components of interest. Lim et al. inserted three different Raman-active molecules into the narrow intrananogap of Au nanoparticles with different subcellular-organelle targeting peptides. The extra enhancement within the nanogap allowed them to create high speed, high resolution multiplexed cellular imaging (Figure 23b).124 Hu et al. carefully designed three 4- ethynylbenzenethiol derivatives (OPE molecules) with different substitution groups. Therefore, these three molecules showed a marked difference in the Raman peak position of the alkyne group. Three color interference-free SERS multiplex cellular imaging has been demonstrated by modifying the three SERS tags with different receptors to anchor to different positions of the cell (Figure 23c).224 They further performed multiplexed 
SERS imaging in single cells for 3D imaging.128 They fabricated nucleus and membrane targeting Au nanoparticles respectively and modified them with different Raman probes. In combination with the confocal Raman system, the high-resolution 3D image of a single cell could be obtained. In addition to cell detection, Gambhir et al. used silica coated Au nanoparticles with four different Raman active molecules to obtain rapid, high-spatial resolution spectroscopic imaging over a wide-area of living mice via their self-designed small animal Raman instrument.225 Chang et al. combined three different lipoic acid-containing NIR active tricarbocyanine reporter molecules for the multiplex imaging of tumor sites in mice226 in 2014. They then utilized easily obtained Raman reporters, including MGITC, Cy5, and R6G modified Au nanoparticles, to perform an in vivo time series multiplexed detection of xenograft tumor biomarkers.227 In summary, all of these multiplex SERS imaging methods resulted in the nonoverlapping peaks of reporter molecules and created images with great detail and clarity for multicomponent analysis. Very recently, Min et al. created a palette of triple bond-conjugated near-infrared dyes with each of them displaying a single peak in the cell-silent Raman spectral window. This palette provided 24 resolvable colors via stimulated Raman scattering, which exemplified the great power of multiplexed cell Raman imaging.228 However, if various colored images were constructed when all of the 24 tags were taken from the same cell, it would be of much interest and significance. A common problem for multiplexed SERS imaging is the limitation in the choice of tags. The overlapping of peaks may occur with the increased number of targets and when the biological system in question becomes increasingly complex. These factors lead to a change in the sensing capability while the SERS peaks of biomolecules simultaneously incite additional overlaps in the presented peaks. To overcome this problem, it is necessary to apply additional Raman molecules possessing distinct peaks and to employ appropriate algorithms that can separate out the necessary information.

3. Results and discussion 
The Raman spectra of most organic molecules and all amino acids, like IR absorption spectra, have a broadly similar form covering a range of about $3 5 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ Raman shift from the excitation laser (Fig. 1). Despite the similar appearance, all the solid-state amino acid spectra are sufficiently different from each other in detail to permit unambiguous identification by spectral database search algorithms. 
Raman spectra are qualitatively identical with different excitation wavelengths, when plotted in wave numbers Raman shift from the excitation line, in this case $5 3 2 \mathrm { n m } = 1 8 7 9 7 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , even though intensities will vary somewhat due to changes in instrument throughput (sensitivity) with wavelength. Similar to infrared absorption spectra, the rather crowded area from ${ \sim } 5 0 0$ to ${ \sim } 1 7 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ Raman shift is known as the “fingerprint region” and contains the majority of the Raman bands used to uniquely identify a particular material. Like human fingerprints, these regions are very complex and in general, they cannot be used directly for structural determination but are valuable for structural confirmation. The majority of the fingerprint bands derive from CH, $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { C H } _ { 3 }$ deformation vibrations, which are omnipresent in organic molecules. Some reasonable guidelines in assigning fingerprint bands to structural features have evolved, largely empirically, over time and these may be used with caution to relate Raman signals to molecular structure. However, the close proximity of the bands and their sensitivity to shifts due to fine structural changes can make the task quite difficult, particularly in mixtures. Many workers utilize the strong and specific Raman shifts observed with isotopic substitution, to isolate and identify specific structural elements within the fingerprint. For example, specific (deuterated) D C bonds will downshift to lower wave numbers and so can be easily detected. 


There is a lacuna from $\mathord { \sim } 1 7 0 0$ to ${ \sim } 2 8 5 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ : this region contains only one main band of interest in natural amino acids and proteins, the thiol SH stretching, at ${ \sim } 2 5 6 0$ to $\sim 2 5 9 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ . From ${ \sim } 2 8 5 0$ to ${ \sim } 3 0 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , a system of highly overlapped bands that results from CH stretching vibrations, often forms the most intense feature of an organic 
Raman spectrum. Experimentally, a steep fall-off in uncorrected CCD detector sensitivity towards the NIR results in the CH bands appearing with less than their true intensity. However, from all but the simplest molecules, the CH stretch range is too convoluted to assist in structurally characterizing a molecule (although it is useful in statistical spectral identification procedures). 
There are also a few higher wave number bands in certain organic materials, for example the aromatic C-H stretch in the region from 3000 to $3 1 0 0 \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ (Fig. 2) and the $\mathrm { N H } _ { 2 }$ stretch in primary amines from 3330 to $3 4 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ . A weak and broad band at about $3 1 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ has been assigned to $\mathrm { N H } ^ { 3 + }$ stretching [15] but is not expected to be of specific value in samples with multiple amino acid components. On the other hand, the imidazole heterocyclic ring structure of histidine (His) can be characterized by two sharp and quite intense bands at ${ \sim } 3 1 1 0$ and ${ \sim } 3 1 6 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ (Fig. 2). His, an essential amino acid, is synthesized by plants and microorganisms, such as Escherichia coli and Salmonella, from phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), each of which contributes part of the ring structure, and from glutamine [16]. Liquid water generates a pair of broad Raman bands, one at about $1 6 0 \bar { 0 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ and another at about $3 4 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ . The presence of crystalline water (hydrated crystals) results in convolution of the $\mathrm { N H } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ stretching bands with a sharper water peak [15]. In the absence of hydration the $\mathrm { N H } _ { 2 }$ stretching band just below $3 4 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ will be more clearly resolved (Fig. 2). 


Liquid water is a rather weak Raman scatterer and does not absorb in the visible, so unlike infrared absorption, does not greatly hinder measurements; it is generally an ideal Raman solvent. Similarly, carbon dioxide in the atmosphere does not cause background absorption problems in Raman measurements. Most Raman spectra can be used “as-is” or with minor cosmetic smoothing and baseline shape correction, and wave number calibration, if required. 
Within the complex fingerprint of many peaks, some organic compounds possess one or two rather strong bands that can be more confidently assigned to molecular structural features. The best known of these is probably the strong ring-breathing vibration in mono-substituted aromatic compounds, found at around $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ . Not surprisingly, this is one of the strongest Raman peaks in the spectrum of Phe (Fig. 3). 

Although both Tyr and Trp contain the aromatic side chain, this strong band at $\mathord { \sim } 1 0 0 0$ is suppressed in Tyr and shifted to ${ \sim } 1 0 1 1$ in Trp due to the different substitution symmetry. However, the para-substituted ring vibration reported at around $8 3 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ [16] is present in the Tyr spectrum in Fig. 4. These two sharp, intense bands serve as excellent markers for the presence of the aromatic residues in complex biopolymers. Fig. 5 shows the clear indication of the three Phe residues in the peptide Bovine insulin B chain. 

The Phe band at $\bar { \sim } 1 0 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ has been used to identify malignant oral tissue in biopsy samples [17]. The possibility clearly exists for the extension of this to in vivo Raman examination of tissue by employing a fiber-optically coupled Raman micro-probe system, as mentioned in the referenced report. In such applications, it is important to select unambiguous Raman bands that appear in the spectrum with good signal to noise and resolution, in order to reduce both error and required laser powers and sampling time. 
The location of the ${ \sim } 8 3 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ ring vibration (sideband at ${ \sim } 8 5 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ ) in Tyr is also subject to variation depending on the exact chemical environment in larger biopolymers, the ${ \sim } 1 0 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ band less so. The provenance of the latter band, as well as the associated side band at about $1 0 3 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , which is an in-plane CH deformation characteristic of monosubstituted benzene ring structures, is clear when the spectrum of toluene is overlapped with that of Phe (Fig. 6). Most of the remaining fingerprint bands in Phe can be attributed to the aliphatic portion of the amino acid. 
Trp is quite strongly fluorescent in green excitation Raman (causing a rising baseline), but unlike fluorescence spectroscopy, the micro-Raman spectra are not affected to the point where they cannot be measured easily. Fig. 7 compares the fingerprint regions Trp and Phe. Another clear characteristic Raman band in the amino acid family derives from the SS stretching deformation in the (oxidized) dimerised cystine, formed by bridging the thiol groups of two cysteine molecules. This generates an intense Raman signal around $5 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ (Fig. 8). 

The exact position of the SS band is determined to some extent by the conformation of the residues contributing the disulfide bridge and hence the protein’s three-dimensional structure. The CS stretching mode in the reduced monomer Cys, as well as reduced Cys-containing proteins, is found over a much wider wave number range from about $5 8 0 { - } 7 4 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , depending on the backbone (primary) molecular structure as well as microenvironment. Crystalline Cys produces a pair of bands, the lower of which is strongly attenuated in solution (Fig. 8). These two bands and the thiol SH stretch at $\sim 2 5 6 0$ to $\mathrm { \stackrel { - } { \sim } } 2 5 9 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ are amongst the most useful and accessible amino acid derived conformational markers in protein structures and have been used to good effect in Raman spectroscopy studies of Salmonella typhimurium proteins [16]. In Fig. 9, the important features of the Cys and cystine spectra are shown in a composite of three spectra. In the oxidized material, the $5 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ SS band is the most intense feature and the CS bands are greatly suppressed. The strong SH band at $2 5 9 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ (shown for a $1 0 0 \mathrm { m m o l }$ aqueous Cys solution) is absent. The broad peak from the water in the Cys sample is also noticeable. Methionine differs from cysteine in having a longer R group terminating in a methyl group instead of a proton. A more complex C-S Raman spectrum is the result (Fig. 10), with a triplet of peaks at about $7 2 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ . 



When amino acid residues polymerize by condensation of a water molecule to form proteins and other biomacromolecules, a peptide or amide bond forms between C and N termini. This amide bond provides a major characteristic of protein structure, particularly the three-dimensional folded structure crucial to protein biochemistry. The general structure of the residue Raman spectral signatures, which largely derive from the side chain, are retained by the peptide or protein, although frequently peaks are less sharply resolved. A trivial case of a homopolymer containing a single residue type is shown for solid Tyr and poly-Tyr in Fig. 10. The strong aromatic ring mode dominates both spectra (although the relative intensities of the doublet peaks are transposed). However, in nature, matters are generally rather more complex. 

Three major “amide” bond Raman active vibrations are known. However, only two are amenable to visible light Raman (amides I and III), the third (amide II) must be excited by deep UV laser light near to its absorption energy in order to enhance the Raman signal by resonance. Amide III is the easiest band to observe as its position at around $1 6 7 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , places it comfortably outside the crowded fingerprint region of protein spectra. The amide bands are also visible in polyamino acids (peptides), homopolymers of a single residue. Fig. 11 shows a comparison of tyrosine, two small peptides (poly-proline and poly-tyrosine), and the natural peptide, insulin B chain, with the positions of the amide III and I bands indicated. The amide III is generally the highest wave number Raman band in the fingerprint of proteins as well as having good intensity Fig. 12. 
4. Conclusions 
Raman spectroscopy was used to study a selection of common amino acids and related biopolymers. Some existing structure assignments were discussed in terms of the observed spectra and the applicability of Raman for characterizing larger biomolecules was examined, based on “building blocks” of amino acid residues. Advantages of micro-Raman spectroscopy are its ability to obtain structurally useful spectra from individual crystals of micrometer scale as well as from aqueous droplets containing of the order of $1 0 ^ { - 6 } \mathrm { m o l }$ or less of a target compound. Indeed, it has been demonstrated that by drying a droplet containing of the order of femtomoles (f mol) of proteins, Raman spectra can be collected [18]. Each amino acid spectrum is unique.

Introduction 
Directly visualizing biological structures and activities at cellular and sub-cellular level remains one of the most intuitive and powerful ways to study biological problems by far.1 Ever since the first microscope was invented in the 17th century, which led to the discoveries of cells and laid the very foundation of the modern understanding of biology, the field of optical microscopy has been advancing rapidly. The emergence of new tools and techniques such as confocal microscopy, super-resolution microscopy and nonlinear microscopy etc. has made it possible for scientists to see and study biology in a noninvasive manner with high spatial-temporal resolution, and thus has expanded our knowledge in life sciences. Among these methods, stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy, is a powerful tool that can generate image contrast of vibrational transitions of chemical bonds with high sensitivity, resolution and speed2–4. Unlike fluorescence microscopy, which generally requires the target to be labeled with a relatively bulky fluorophore, SRS microscopy requires no label or only minimal labels that better preserve the structure and function of the small molecules and are more resistant to photobleaching. When compared to another Raman imaging technique, Coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy (CARS), SRS is also free from non-resonant background and has linear signal dependence on analyte concentration, which makes it well suited for quantitative studies that are of immense importance for answering biological questions.5, 6 
Label-free imaging has long been adopted for SRS microscopy and vibrational imaging in general, because it doesn’t require any exogenous labeling and reflects native cellular metabolic states.7–9 The very nature of label-free imaging techniques permits such applications to be performed in vivo. Chemical bonds such as O–P–O, $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { O }$ , $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { C }$ , $\mathrm { S } { = } \mathrm { O }$ , O–H, C–H are frequently probed, especially $\mathrm { C - H }$ as it is highly enriched in lipids and proteins – the most abundant biomolecules in the cell – and thus gives the highest signal. More importantly, the rich spectral features that vary between different molecules makes it possible for hyperspectral imaging of multiple chemical species that are always of great interest to biologists. In recent advances with label-free techniques, for example, metabolic heterogeneity of live Euglena gracilis has been studied10, providing insight to microalgal research; in other studies, neurotransmitter11 and neuronal membrane potential12 have been visualized, adding new tools to investigate neurobiology; and brain tumor infiltration diagnostics13, 14 has been successfully demonstrated in mouse brain and human patient samples, and an intraoperative set-up using fiber laser was then engineered15 to assist surgery. However, although label-free vibrational imaging has been demonstrated a useful tool in biological studies, the detection specificity is usually limited – any molecules that harbor the same chemical bond of target will have severely overlapping spectrum and make it extremely hard to image a specific molecule of interest. 
For the above reason, Raman/vibrational tags have been developed to circumvent the endogenous cellular background and enable specific detection of the chemical species of interest. This is achieved by introducing chemical bonds that vibrate in the cell-silent Raman window $( 1 8 0 0 - 2 6 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ , in which no endogenous molecules vibrate. There are several benefits associated with using vibrational tags. Stable isotope substitution (such as $^ 2 \mathrm { H }$ and $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ ) has been long exploited in NMR, mass spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy. The substituted molecules are almost chemically identical to the unsubstituted, and thus have good metabolic labeling efficiency. Another alternative is to label molecules of interest with tiny vibrational tags such as nitrile and alkyne. These tags also have unique vibrational frequencies in the cell silent window, and have much larger Raman scattering cross sections to generate strong signal, which is another major advantage of using vibrational tags. Generally, two labeling strategies are associated with these labeled molecules: steady-state or pulse-chase labeling. For the steady-state strategy, labeled molecules are added long enough until the incorporation approaches steady-state, and information such as spatial distribution and incorporation rate can be obtained; while for the pulse-chase labeling strategy, labeled molecules are added for a certain amount of time and then removed, and the decay of the tags can be traced to provide additional turnover kinetics. By these methods complex dynamic information could be obtained which is hard to extract from label-free approach. Furthermore, the introduced vibrational tags can be manipulated in terms of vibrational frequencies, which makes multi-color imaging feasible. There are advantages and disadvantages associated with stable isotope substitution and tiny vibrational tags. Isotope substitutions are chemically identical to the original forms, and the kinetic isotope effect is usually negligible for the duration of typical experiments. Thus, the incorporation to their metabolites is the same as the original forms. But the Raman cross sections of these tags are small, and the signal from these tags is weak. For the above reasons, isotope substitution is ideal for imaging small but abundant biomolecules that are easily perturbed by structural alteration. Other vibrational tags such as alkyne on the other hand usually have much larger Raman cross sections, and yield a large signal at low concentration. Yet the alkyne moiety introduces structural alternation to the molecules and could potentially alter the chemical activity16. And therefore it is usually necessary to test the bioactivity when labeling a molecule with alkyne moiety. 

In this article, we review recent applications of Raman imaging with vibrational tags, with an emphasis on SRS, on life sciences such as cellular metabolism of nucleic acid, protein, lipid, glucose, small molecule imaging such as drug, and organelle imaging, as well as brain and tumor metabolism. We hope we can convey the potential of SRS imaging of vibrational tags on biological studies especially the ones focusing on cellular metabolism and small molecule imaging. 
Nucleic Acid Metabolism 
In this section, we review the application of vibrational tags to interrogate nucleic acid metabolism. Conventionally nucleic acids can be visualized by helix-intercalating dyes such as DAPI or Hoechst or hybridization-based techniques. However, metabolic imaging of nucleic acids reveals more information on the dynamic aspect, which is dependent on cell activity. For example, new DNA synthesis reflects cell proliferation, while the RNA turnover is considered as a regulatory control over protein level. Traditionally, measuring DNA synthesis was achieved by nucleoside analog bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU), which can then be detected using antibody against BrdU. Later, the development of bioorthogonal chemistry introduced alkyne as a chemical handle into a deoxyuridine (dU) analog, 5-ethynyl deoxyuridine (EdU)17. However, these methods either cannot work with live cells, or suffer from non-specific membrane staining background. 
Raman imaging is then recognized as the suitable tool to visualize the alkyne-tagged nucleoside analogs without further modification or click-chemistry reaction. Along this, Yamakoshi et al. demonstrated imaging of EdU incorporated in DNA by spontaneous Raman micro-spectroscopy in living cells18 (Figure 1A). To further boost the imaging speed and sensitivity and achieve live cell imaging, Wei et al. and Hong et al. independently applied stimulated Raman scattering and captured the newly synthesized DNA in living cells19, 20 (Figure 1B–C). Wei et al. also successfully probed cell proliferation in $C .$ elegans germline19 (Figure 1D). Later Chen et al. created different vibrational colors for EdU by isotope-editing the alkyne moiety21 (Figure 1E–F). With these multi-color labels and applying them in a pulse-chase manner, Hu et al. recently showed that even different stages of DNA synthesis could be visualized in the same nuclei of neural progenitor $\mathrm { c e l l } ^ { 2 2 }$ (Figure 1G–I). Thus, the live-cell imaging capability of SRS as well as the multiplexing potential of EdU makes it possible to reveal cell cycle dynamics in complex tissue or animal samples. 
Using the similar strategy, RNA synthesis can be measured by incorporation of alkynetagged uridine analog, 5-ethynyl uridine (EU)23. Employing SRS imaging, Wei et al. visualized RNA synthesis, most of which is attributed to ribosomal RNA19. With pulsechase labeling, they also showed that compared to DNA dynamics at the time scale of a cell cycle, RNA turnover is much faster (Figure 1J). 
Protein Metabolism 
As the last piece in central dogma, protein metabolism is tightly controlled via both synthesis and degradation. Some modalities of measuring protein dynamics have been developed, such as genetically encoded GFP reporter24 and SILAC-based protein mass spectrometry25. The former fuses GFP to a specific protein, which enables fluorescence imaging and quantification of one protein at a time24. It allows spatial information to be obtained in live cells, but is only limited to selected proteins and does not report the global protein homeostasis. The latter uses isotope-labeled amino acids to create mass shift in peptides, which marks the newly synthesized proteins in mass spectrometry25.

INTRODUCTION 
Investigation of protein structure by Raman spectroscopy has been practised for more than three decades, during which specific band assignments, signatures of secondary structure1 and Raman markers of side-chain environments2 have been established. The basic principles and experimental aspects of Raman spectroscopy of proteins and their complexes were recently reviewed.3–5 Similarly, a comprehensive and in-depth survey of available instrumentation can be found in a recent book.6 The wide deployment of chargecoupled device (CCD) detectors and holographic filters within the last decade has dramatically increased the achievable signal-to-noise ratio in Raman spectra. This has made digital difference spectroscopy applicable to dilute protein solutions. Difference spectroscopy has emerged as an indispensable tool for detecting minute structural changes.7–9 A new fiber sampling technique has shown promise to permit the collection of Raman spectra from submicromolar protein solutions.10 The improved sensitivity also facilitated applications of Raman microspectroscopy and extraction of ligand-binding details from crystalline samples.11 

These developments and versatile commercial Raman instrumentation have permitted new applications in characterizing proteins in biotechnology, pharmaceutical production and the food industry. This trend is likely to continue and will drive the need for the quantitative interpretation of protein spectra. Traditionally, the positions and intensities of amide bands, which arise from coupled vibrational modes of the polypeptide backbone, were used for empirical estimations of secondary structure. The estimates rested on the analysis of the amide bands using spectral decompositions or deconvolution of the complex and broad envelopes into a few component bands (recently reviewed12,13). The decomposed bands were then related to a set of reference spectra collected from proteins with known three-dimensional structures and the fractions of secondary structure $\scriptstyle { \alpha }$ -helix, $\beta$ -strand, turns, disordered) were computed.14 – 17 The accuracy of these methods is generally comparable to the similar analysis of circular dichroism spectra and provides results that are certainly better than the sequence-based estimates. However, these methods employ unwarranted assumptions about intrinsic Raman and IR intensities and tend to underestimate spectral overlaps between marker for different secondary structures.18 

Fortunately, the rapid increase in computational capacity and the availability of suitable model compounds has been driving steady progress in ab initio vibrational analyses.19 – 21 This renewed interest has also been fueled by the advent of two-dimensional (pump-and-probe) vibrational spectroscopy which allowed an experimental determination of the nearest-neighbor coupling constants in model peptides.22,23 These coupling constants are akin to the dipolar couplings determined by NMR and constitute essential parameters for structure determination and spectral simulations. Recently, it was demonstrated that simulated vibrational wavenumbers and intensities could be used to determine conformations of short peptides from Raman and IR spectra.24 – 28 A similar amide I mode description has been used to simulate IR amide I envelopes of proteins with reasonable success.18 Although the information extractable from the amide bands alone is not sufficient for three-dimensional structure determination, one can envision Raman-assisted database comparisons used for fold classification and Raman-assisted modeling of structural changes and homologous proteins.29 
Generally, analysis of the side-chain marker bands is far from quantitative. Because the Raman intensities of side-chain bands depend strongly on the side-chain environments it is considerably more difficult to model the spectra computationally. However, even qualitative constraints can be valuable when carefully combined with homology modeling and molecular mechanics.29,30 
In this review, we first turn our attention to the theoretical and experimental progress in vibrational analyses of amide modes. We then survey novel side-chain assignments and structure–spectra correlations. Raman investigations of natively unfolded proteins, protein crystals and assemblies are discussed in applications. Applications of Raman difference spectroscopy in enzymology are also included. Finally, a host of biotechnology and biomedical applications are mentioned to illustrate the versatility of the techniques and to stress the need to close the gap between theoretical and research laboratory developments and deployment of Raman technology in industry. Given the breath of the topic, this review is not intended to provide an exhaustive compilation of the existing literature. Instead, it was approached from the position of a protein chemist who tries to identify the key advances and developments that may bring new applications of Raman spectroscopy to the biotechnology laboratory. 

SPECTRAL ASSIGNMENTS ANDINTERPRETATION TECHNIQUES
All spectroscopic applications in structural biology rest on reliable assignments of the spectral features and on correlations between the band positions and intensities and the structure (i.e. structure marker bands). The assignments are usually based on model compounds (e.g. amino acids or short peptides) and may be universal for the whole class of molecules (e.g. amide bands of proteins are assigned to polypeptide backbone modes). Many assignments have been established for proteins throughout the years (reviewed in Refs 2–4) and here we focus only on the recent developments. A typical protein spectrum together with the assignments of the most prominent spectral features and selected marker bands is shown in Fig. 1. 
Protein backbone assignments 
Progress in polypeptide normal mode analysis Because proteins are large polypeptides, often consisting of hundreds of amino acids, their vibrational spectra contain a complex set of overlapping bands. However, Raman scattering of aromatic amino acids and the polypeptide chain is intrinsically strong and gives rise to a set of dominant peaks in the spectrum (see assignments in Fig. 1). For example, the strong peak at $1 6 5 6 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ is the so-called amide I band that corresponds to the sum of coupled modes of the polypeptide backbone.1 A major contribution to the amide I modes comes from the ${ \mathrm { C } } { = } \mathrm { O }$ stretching of the peptide carbonyl groups.1 The amide III mode is another coupled vibration of the polypeptide backbone, mainly resulting from the coupled $_ \mathrm { C - N }$ stretching and $_ \mathrm { N - H }$ bending motions1 (Fig. 1). 

The peptide carbonyl groups act as acceptors of hydrogen bonds within ordered secondary structure, thus making the position of the amide I band strongly dependent on the backbone secondary and tertiary structure. In addition, vibrational coupling between motions of different peptide groups within an ordered structure causes excitonic coupling of the amide I modes and produces further spectral shifts.31 The coupling has been computationally described in terms of transition dipole coupling (TDC), e.g. throughspace electrostatic interactions.21 However, recent ab initio calculations and model dipeptide studies demonstrated that through-bond interactions, e.g. nearest-neighbor couplings, are more important than the through-space TDC.19,20,32,33 The authors invoked Hessian matrix reconstruction to appraise the influence of the through bond and through space couplings on the local amide I modes.20 They also found that the local amide I modes depend strongly on the position within sequence whereas the nearest neighbor coupling terms are sequence independent and quantitatively transferable from dipeptides to longer polypeptides.20 This, in effect, opens a way for an ab initio calculation of the coupling constants using dipeptide models. The calculated coupling constants can be compared with the experimental values obtained by 2D IR spectroscopy34 in order to adjust the scaling and appraise solvent effects. The corrected constants, may, in principle, yield the correct amide I envelope for any given protein.20 
An explicit exciton coupling framework has been developed for tripeptides and utilizes combination of IR and polarized Raman spectra to derive the coupling parameters between the two amide I modes observed for these short oligopeptides.24,26 The theoretical framework eventually yields the $\phi$ and $\psi$ angles for the tripeptide.35 This elegant methodology was then used to elucidate the solution structure of various tripeptides.25,27,28,36 The treatment was extended to incorporate constraints from other spectroscopic techniques like electronic and vibrational circular dichroism (VCD).37,38 The theory was subsequently extended to a tetrapeptide, i.e. a three-oscillator model, and used to determine the preferred conformation of tetraalanine in water28 (Fig. 2). In this case, the authors exploited global spectral decomposition of the ${ \mathrm { I R } } ,$ isotropic and anisotropic Raman spectra to resolve contributions of the three expected amide $\mathrm { I ^ { \prime } }$ modes. In addition, the dihedral angles were verified by comparing the simulated and the experimental VCD contour (Fig. 2, bottom panel). 
Because this method relies on the spectral decomposition by a curve fitting, the results become less reliable with every additional peptide bond. Hence the same approach is unlikely to yield a unique solution for larger polypeptides. However, the method has been instrumental in addressing very important issues in protein folding, namely the intrinsic conformational preferences in polypeptides and the prefered conformations adopted by an unfolded chain.27 The combination of IR, Raman and VCD with the theoretical framework has also been useful in providing novel amide I assignments.36 These are important results, which paved the way for the concerted interpretation of different spectroscopic results using a unified theoretical framework. As many biotechnology centers enlarge their instrument assets and spectroscopic capabilities, this approach will definitely become common and appropriate tools needs to be developed and evaluated.

Introduction 
The goal of this structural study of proteins is to gain insight into the overall structure of these compounds without establishing the precise three-dimensional localization of individual structural elements. With Raman spectroscopy, several vibrational modes can be used for the analysis of peptide structure. Most characteristic bands are associated with the CONH group, referred to as amide A (NH stretching, about $3 5 0 0 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 } )$ , amide B (NH stretching, about $3 1 0 0 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ ) and amide I to VII (I: $1 6 0 0 { - } 1 6 9 0 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ , II: $1 4 8 0 { - } 1 5 8 0 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ , III: 1230– $1 3 0 0 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ , IV: $6 2 5 { - } 7 7 0 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ , V: $6 4 0 { - } 8 0 0 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ , VI: $5 4 0 { - } 6 0 0 { \ c m } ^ { - 1 }$ VII: $2 0 0 \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ ).[1] The following three signals are of main interest for the identification of different protein backbone confirmations: amide I (stretching vibration of $\mathsf C = { \mathsf O } )$ , amide II and amide III (both associated with coupled C–N stretching and N–H bending vibrations of the peptide group).[2] The assignment of the remaining peptide modes is accordingly, amide IV (OCN bending), amide V (out-of-plane NH bending), amide VI (out-of-plane $\mathsf C = \mathsf { O }$ bending) and amide VII (skeletal mode). The wavenumber of amide modes reflects the structure of the main polypeptide chain irrespective of side groups. 
A special interest is directed to the secondary structure of proteins. Among the most important groups of proteins, we can include the $\propto$ -helix and the $\beta$ -sheet structures. Raman spectrosa bcopy of protein secondary structure has followed the approach taken by CD studies. It has focused on the correlation of the position of the amide I and amide III vibrations with the crystallographically determined fraction of each secondary structural element present in protein. Typical wavenumbers for -helix and $\beta$ -sheet structures are: 1662–1655 and $1 2 7 2 - 1 2 6 4  c m ^ { - 1 }$ $( \alpha )$ , b1674–1672 and $1 2 4 2 - 1 2 2 7  c m ^ { - 1 }$ a( ), respectively, for amide I and amide III modes.[3] 
Quantitative methodology for determining protein secondary structure was also demonstrated, and Raman method appeared to be complementary to CD, VCD and absorption spectroscopy.[4] The pH-induced conformational change[5] and protein dynamics at various incubation times[6] were recorded with two-dimensional 
Raman correlation spectroscopy. Raman spectroscopic characterization can be applied to proteins in various states: aqueous (dilute) solution (the $H _ { 2 } O$ bending vibration mode that obscures the amide I band in IR spectroscopy has low intensity in the Raman spectra), precipitates fibrils, amorphous aggregates, solids and crystals.[7] With Raman Optical Activity (ROA), also the motif and fold of proteins in solution can be investigated.[8] The extreme sensitivity of the surface enhanced resonance Raman method (SERRS) was demonstrated for glucose oxidase at the silver electrode with the release of free flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) detected from a solution at concentrations as low as $1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } M$ .[9] 
In addition to the characterization of the amide bands, there are additional features in the Raman spectra that permit the description of the environment of numerous amino acid chains. These include the amino acid side-chain modes (e.g. tryptophan doublet $1 3 6 0 / 1 3 4 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , tyrosine doublet $8 6 0 / 8 3 3 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ ) or the sulfur-containing residues in the different physical states (C–S stretching with $\mathsf { H }$ at the trans position of the S atom: $6 4 0 { - } 6 8 0 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ and C–S stretching with C at the trans position of the S atom; $7 4 0 { - } 7 6 0 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ , S–S stretching: $5 0 8 { - } 5 1 2 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ (GGG), $5 2 3 { - } 5 2 8 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ (TGT), $5 4 0 { - } 5 4 5 { \mathsf { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ (TGT)).[3] 
Raman spectroscopy shows strong potential for providing noninvasive information from various samples important in biology and medicine.[2] Different techniques (e.g. UVRR, ROA) were successfully applied for pharmaceutical studies including protein– protein interaction, protein aggregation and conformation.[10] Raman spectroscopy is especially useful when the analysis can also be based on the spectra measured from isolated substances. 
In spite of the fact that Raman spectra show characteristic fingerprints, which can be used for molecular identification, the spectral profile strongly depends on the wavenumber of the laser excitation (as shown for three exemplary proteins in Figs. 1–3). The difference can be related to the characteristic optical response of the spectrometers and the detector used. The decrease of the Raman intensity above the fingerprint range may be caused by lower sensitivity of the silicon CCD detection with regard to NIR radiation.[11] Raman scattering is a weak phenomenon, but when the resonance take place (Fig. 2), the effect in which the exciting laser wavelength is adjusted to the absorption range of particular chromophore within the sample, the significant sensitivity enhancement for vibrational modes of this group is observed.[3] By selecting an appropriate excitation wavelength, different chromophores of the same molecule can be monitored. In particular, resonance Raman spectrum of heme proteins allows the selective enhancement of different vibrational modes at different wavelengths and monitoring the heme structural changes associated with, e.g. the oxygen binding or the electron transfer.[12] However, in some cases, the fluorescence may obscure the Raman spectrum (Fig. 3), and only the measurement at the longer excitation wavelength is reasonable. 

In this work, 26 proteins of different structure, function and properties are investigated by Raman spectroscopy with 488, 532 and $1 0 6 4 \mathsf { n m }$ laser lines. To discuss their spectral properties, proteins were divided, according to the Structural Classification of Proteins (SCOP),[13] into four classes according to their secondary structure, i.e. $\scriptstyle { \varnothing } ^ { \prime }$ -helical $( \alpha )$ , $\beta$ -sheet ( ), mixed structures $( \alpha / \beta ,$ $\alpha + \beta , \ s )$ a a b b a b and others. Several reviews (e.g.[3,6,14]) showing the a bpotential of Raman (and IR, e.g.[15]) spectroscopy for the measurement and analysis of proteins have been published; however, to the best of our knowledge, such a large collection of individual protein Raman spectra was not offered in any paper. This work can serve as a review and comprehensive vibrational spectra library, based on our and previous Raman measurements, with detailed analysis.

Conclusions 
Alkene hydrocarbon stapling is used frequently in chemical biology and drug discovery to conformationally constrain peptides to adopt their helical bioactive conformation and improve their physicochemical properties. However, there are several issues with $i , i + 7$ stapled peptides that still need to be addressed. We report here the development of a new diynegirder stapling strategy with several advantages, including the requirement for only one type of unnatural amino acid and produces a single isomer on macrocyclisation. The optimal amino acid stereochemistry and diyne hydrocarbon bridge length was investigated through the asymmetric synthesis of nine Fmoc alkyne amino acids with varying lengths and stereochemistries. An $S _ { 7 } S _ { 7 }$ hydrocarbon staple including α- methyl groups was found to be the most helical. Proteolytic stability studies confirmed that the stapled analogues were more stable than their native counterpart. Fluorescence microscopy determined that the alkene and diyne stapled analogues were able to penetrate cells, whilst the native could not. Furthermore, we envisioned that the diyne-girder constraint may show Raman activity in the cell silent region, which could be useful for cell imaging. We have determined that the diynegirder stapled peptide has a significant peak in the cell silent region $( 1 , 8 0 0 - 2 , 8 0 0 ~ \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ using solid-state Raman spectroscopy. Our current and future investigations will focus on the application of diyne-girder stapled peptides, including the development of an i, $i + 1 1$ diyne-girder staple, for the regulation of protein-protein interactions and their visualisation in cells using confocal Raman imagining.

3. Result and discussion 
Our initial experiment sought to establish the spectral characteristics of multiple types of protein at single-molecule concentration. The comparison between orientation-dependent protein Raman signatures is valid only after single molecule detection is established. Bi-analyte analysis, being the only reliable method to ensure that a SERS spectrum being indeed from one single molecule, is utilized for both peptides (Neurotensin (8-13) and Substance P (7-11)) and proteins (Human MANF/ARMET Protein and Human CD137/4-1BB Protein). At around $1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathbf { M }$ concentration of analytes, we observed spectral responses from over $8 5 \%$ of SERS hotspots to be of only one type of bio-molecule, firmly establishing the single-molecule detection capability. 100 Raman spectra were collected from individual molecules of each sample. All spectra were normalized by the highest peak to rule out the impact of incident light intensity. Figs. 1 and 2 show the average Normalized Raman intensities of peptides and proteins from bi-analyte analyses, respectively. Common predominant peaks in proteins occurred at 850 (Tyr), 1000 (Phe), 1140 (C-N bonding), 1360 (Tyr) and 1386 $\mathrm { ( C H } _ { 3 } )$ $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ . The orientation difference does not affect the position of Raman peaks as evidenced by our experimental results shown in Figs. 1 and 2. The only factor leading to the normalized spectral difference between 
individual molecules of the same protein is orientation. 
To illustrate the underlying reason for the observed trend, we show the polarization configuration in Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 4). The Raman peak intensity is proportional to the incident light intensity as well as the cosine of the angle between the polarization direction of the EM field of local plasmon resonance and the orientation of the Raman active bond. As normalization was done to rule out the impact of laser intensity variation and plasmon resonance intensity, the relation shown in Fig. 3a can be obtained for the Raman peak intensity of individual Raman active bonds. When multiple bonds of the same type exist within one hotspot, multiple angles contribute additively to the observed peak intensity (Fig. 3b). As the number of bonds increases, the values of cosine function of different angles “counteract” each other, leading to a convergence in standard deviation. 

Standard deviation was used to show the intensity variation of individual protein molecules. To make peak comparison meaningful, we define the change in intensity using the absolute change in intensity divided by the normalized average peak intensity. For each type of protein we tested, standard deiation of Raman peak intensity was calculated for multiple wavenumbers, including Tyr $( 8 5 0 ~ \mathrm { ~ c m } ^ { - 1 }$ and $1 3 6 0 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } } \mathrm { { . } }$ ), Phe $( 1 0 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } ) }$ , C-N bonding $( 1 1 4 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )  { \mathrm { ~ \textrm ~ { ~ ~ } ~ } } .$ ) and CH3 $( 1 3 8 6 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } $ ) were calculated (Fig. 4). The X-axis of the figure represents the atomic weight of the substances ranging from Substance P (5 amino acid (aa)), Neurotensin (6aa) to Human MANF (182aa) and Human CD137 (255aa). In Substance P peptide, Tyrosine only appears once in the peptide structure and the standard deviation for the Tyrosine characteristic peak is 0.25. The two types of protein (Human MANF and Human CD137) have multiple Tyrosine in their protein structure, showing a low standard deviation of $0 . 0 6 { - } 0 . 0 7$ . Similar situation happens to the amino acid Phenylalanine. The standard deviation for Phe in Neurotensin peptide (2 Phe in its structure) is 0.18 while the standard deviation is 0.06–0.07 for the two proteins. For the two peptides (Substance P and Neurotensin), the reason for their difference in amino acid characteristic peak is that Substance P contains only 1 Tyr while Neurotensin contains 2 Phe, leading to the two amino acid orientation counteract against one another. MANF and CD137 shows almost same deviation difference in peak corresponding to the 2 types of amino acid (Tyr and Phe). The two types of bonds ( $\mathrm { C H } _ { 3 }$ and CN) appears in every amino acid, and this leads to smaller standard deviation than the two amino acids, which appears less frequently in the proteins. A clear trend of convergence in standard deviation with increasing protein size is observed. It can be concluded that orientation has less impact on spectral signature as the size of the molecules becomes larger. 

We performed simulation (see materials and methods) to validate the physics model (Fig. 5). Amino acid number from 1 to 13 were simulated using 13 groups of random cosine number (each group consists of 1000 random number from 0 to 1) to simulate the random orientation of Raman active bonds on SERS substrate relative to the incident light direction. The simulation was repeated five times to ensure reproducibility. We then calculated and plotted the standard deviation to compare with experimental results. Relative standard deviation so obtained ranges from 0.32 to 0.07 for random angles with a sharp decrease as amino acid number increases from 1 to 7 and the decrease becomes slower and eventually stops at 12 amino acids. From the three distributions at amino acid number 1, 6 and 13, we attribute the decrease in standard deviation to the trend of uniformity in summation of the values of cosine function with random angles. We find similar trends between simulation and experimental result (Fig. 4). Comparison between Figs. 4 and 5 shows that experimental results render smaller standard deviation than simulation results. This could conceivably be due to the existence of preferred orientation of the bio molecules e.g. lying parallel to the substrate surface due presumably to non-zero attraction between the surface and the molecules. The simulation results should be taken as the upper limit for the standard deviation of normalized peak intensity for in vivo testing, that is when the orientation is truly random without any orientation preference. 

Amide III peaks containing secondary structure information of proteins such as protein-protein interaction and conformational changes are of vital importance for the study of protein functionality. Human MANF protein is located on the short arm of human chromosome 3 and the secondary structure is dominated by $\alpha$ -helix [16]. CD137, on the other hand, is expressed by activated $\mathrm { T }$ cells, and is dominated by $\beta$ -sheet structure [17]. The contrast in spectral features of these two types of protein is a good example for the capability of monitoring protein secondary structure variation in the presence of protein orientation change. By zooming in on the spectral region of $1 1 8 0 { - } 1 3 2 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ of the averaged Raman spectra of all four types of proteins at single molecule concentration, Amide III peak is clearly visible as shown in Fig. 6a. Peak corresponding to $\beta$ -sheet $( 1 2 3 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ , random $( 1 2 5 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ ) and $\alpha$ -helix $( 1 3 2 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } ) $ ) were all marked in the figure. Human MANF protein has a high $1 3 2 0 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ peak while CD137 protein has a high $1 2 3 0 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ peak, which is in accordance with their secondary structures. When evaluating the orientation impact on secondary structure detection of protein using SERS, the standard deviation was calculated for the three important Amide III peaks as is shown in Fig. 6b. The highest value (0.062) of standard deviation appears for the Substance P $\beta$ -sheet $( 1 2 3 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ ) peak with the comparable value of the $\alpha$ -helix $( 1 3 2 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ ) peak and (0.061) of Neurotensin. The secondary structure deviation does not change with the increase of molecular weight, indicating that the $\alpha$ -helix, $\beta$ -sheet and random coil are all stable regardless of protein type. All other peaks are of the standard deviation value lower than 0.06, which can be regarded as experimental uncertainty, and the value does not show amino acid number (molecular weight) dependence. Compared with the simulation results in Fig. 5, all the standard deviation values of Amide III are below the convergence value calculated by simulation. This shows that the Amide III peaks are stable for all protein tested. This observation indicates that SERS is a promising method in understanding protein secondary structure. 
We have shown through experimental studies and simulation that for biomedically relevant protein, the distribution of the various angles of amino acids over SERS surfaces is not expected to degrade the specificity of protein identification. The four types of protein all show a high degree of uniformity in protein signature. 

4. Conclusion 
Hundreds of SERS spectra from randomly oriented single molecules are systematically studied with emphasis on the impact of molecular orientation on SERS spectral features. The single-molecule nature of each of the SERS spectra is ensured via bi-analyte analysis, which is in turn made possible by the single-molecule sensitivity of the SERS substrate employed. The molecules are dispersed over the SERS substrate surface with their orientation being distributed stochastically. The standard deviation in peak intensity of common peaks of amino acids is shown to be dependent monotonically on the size (and thus the number of amino acids) of individual protein molecules with orders of magnitude smaller standard deviation from proteins containing more than 13 amino acids. Numerical simulation has shown that orientation has little impact on SERS peak intensity variation of protein with more than 13 amino acids and have no impact on secondary structure detection regardless of protein size, consistent with the experimental observations. This study offers a plausible explanation of the reason that the random orientation of biomedically relevant proteins does not hinder the repeatedly demonstrated specificity of SERS in identification of biological entities including proteins, exosomes and cells. This work provides a solid foundation for propelling SERS into an important tool for biomedical applications.

Discussion 
In summary, we adapted a Raman microscope to demonstrate Raman imaging of small living subjects while using two different types of Raman nanoparticles, SERS active nanoparticles (Nanoplex Biotags), and SWNTs. We have shown relatively high signal reproducibility both in vitro and in living subjects and the ability to produce an image of nanoparticles from both s.c. locations and from deeper tissues (e.g., liver) in living mice. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the ability to follow the arrival of nanoparticles in liver tissue to create time–activity curves. A minimum detection sensitivity of $8 . 1 2 5 \mathrm { p M }$ was observed in a living mouse while using SERS nanoparticles. The ability to multiplex with four SERS nanoparticles presenting different Raman spectra was also demonstrated with the rapid and straightforward distinction between these nanoparticles in living mice. These initial results are encouraging and demonstrate the potential robustness of a Raman-based imaging strategy for small living subjects. 

In the current proof-of-principle work, we demonstrated detection of Raman nanoparticles in both superficial and deep tissues along with an initial evaluation of its potential to detect tumor targeting with SWNTs conjugated to RGD peptide in an U87MG animal model. The primary limitation to Raman imaging of larger subjects will be those also faced by other optical techniques and is limited by NIR light penetration beyond a few centimeters of tissue (17). The key advantages of the current Raman imaging strategy over fluorescence is the very high multiplexing capability and lack of confounding background signal from autofluorescence. A study by Souza et al. (18) was able to collect a Raman spectra from the surface of a mouse (without forming any images) but had to use intratumoral injection of nanoparticles and also a very large concentration $( 3 . 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ of Raman nanoparticles in a relatively large volume of $3 0 0 \mu \mathrm { l }$ (18). Another group has applied multiple Raman signals to follow the distribution of cholesterol in a rat eye while showing the phenotyping of lymphocytes by using a single nonenhanced Raman-labeled (filipin) polystyrene bead to monitor cholesterol in a rat eye in conjunction with the inherent Raman peak associated with proteins to follow the distribution of cholesterol (19). Furthermore, it was shown that these Raman-labeled polystyrene spheres could be successfully used in combination with a fluorescent label. Using an additional Raman label, can overcome the many limitations that arise with fluorescence such as photobleaching, autofluorescence, and a limited number of fluorescent labels. Although we demonstrated multiplexing with only four SERS nanoparticles, we should be able to easily image many more simultaneously injected SERS nanoparticles, and as many as 10 spectrally distinct SERS nanoparticles are already available (e.g., Oxonica). 
Glass-encapsulated SERS active nanoparticles are only one kind of Raman particle recently developed that can be used as contrast agents for molecular imaging. Roughened surface noble metal nanoparticles labeled with binding affinity molecules have also been shown to dramatically increase the Raman signal of their complementary molecules once attached through the SERS mechanism (12, 20, 21). Conjugation of monoclonal antibodies with SERS nanoparticles for targeting and imaging of specific cancer markers in live cultured cells was also recently investigated (5). Another study presents the first in vivo application of SERS for glucose measurements in a rat (22) by s.c. implantation of functionalized SERS nanospheres. 
Recent publications have reviewed the rapid increase of Raman spectroscopy in many biomedical applications (23–25). One report has demonstrated the ability of Raman spectroscopy to diagnose benign and malignant excised breast tissue with high sensitivity and specificity (26). Another article discusses the potential of Raman spectroscopy to analyze the morphologic composition of atherosclerotic coronary artery lesions and assess plaque instability and disease progression in vivo (27). The recent development of a highly efficient Raman optical fiber probe has now bridged the gap between Raman spectroscopy and the clinical setting. The optical fiber probe has successfully demonstrated its usefulness in assessing human tissue models for disease and thus has great potential as a clinically practical technique (28, 29). In particular, this Raman optical fiber probe has the potential of being an extremely useful tool in an intraoperative setting, for instance in surgical debulking of cancers. Its ultra-high sensitivity would be useful in detecting even the smallest presence of malignant tissues in the human body for excision. By using targeted SERS nanoparticles and noninvasive in vivo imaging, Raman spectroscopy can become an important clinical diagnostic tool, as demonstrated in this article. 

Biodistribution of these Raman nanoparticles are currently being evaluated in our lab with the use of radiolabels (e.g., with positron emitters) so that quantification of exact nanoparticle concentration can be explored as we have recently done with radiolabeled quantum dots (30). Additional work with tissue targeting of the Raman nanoparticles (SERS and SWNTS) should also help to further expand the eventual utility of the strategies developed in this work. Further studies with both SERS and SWNTS will still be needed to understand any potential limitations, including delivery due to nanoparticle size, optimal injected dose, and potential for toxicity. Just as quantum dots are finding increasing applications for imaging of small-animal models (31–33), so should Raman nanoparticles lead to increasing applications without the limitations faced by conventional fluorescence imaging. Furthermore, the high sensitivity associated with our modified Raman microscope in conjunction with SERS nanoparticles $\left( 8 . 1 2 5 \ \mathrm { p M } \right)$ represents an important advantage over the sensitivity of conventional fluoroscopy imaging devices in conjunction with quantum dots $[ \approx 1 1 \mathrm { n M }$ using IVIS (Xenogen) and Maestro (CRi, Inc.) imaging systems (unpublished data)]. Additional comparisons between quantum dots and Raman nanoparticles should help to further demonstrate the true advantages of each technique. Although no single molecular imaging strategy (including Raman) is optimal for all biological models, the use of the current Raman imaging strategy along with existing optical and nonoptical strategies should help expand the available toolbox for the field of molecular imaging. In addition, we are developing new Raman spectroscopy instrumentation for dedicated imaging of small living subjects, which should lead to faster image acquisition times; the potential to estimate signal depth; and, eventually, tomographic imaging. Further optimized instrumentation and more studies with various Raman nanoparticles should help to markedly expand the use of Raman imaging of small living subjects and should also impact newer clinical imaging strategies. The current work sets the foundation for future studies and supports continued investigation of Raman imaging of living subjects.

[Subsection] 5.4. Fluorescence Correlation Spectroscopy 
Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) has emerged as a powerful technique for directly measuring the cytosolic concentration of fluorescently labeled CPPs. Briefly, FCS measures the fluorescence intensity in a small volume of a sample that is at equilibrium. The observed intensity fluctuates as a function of time as fluorescent molecules diffuse into and out of the small volume, giving rise to an autocorrelation function. This autocorrelation function relates to the duration of intensity fluctuations and can be correlated to the sample concentration by calculating the number of molecules that entered the viewing area.368 Weizenegger et al. employed FCS to evaluate the uptake efficiency of penetratin and an FGFderived membrane translocating sequence (MTs) at low nanomolar concentrations and found that penetratin was internalized ${ \sim } 3$ -fold better than MTS.369 Schepartz and colleagues further expanded the study to a larger set of cationic CPPs and stapled peptides.370 Incubation of HeLa cells with $5 0 0 \ \mathrm { \ n M }$ rhodamine-labeled peptides resulted in intracellular concentrations of $3 5 0 ~ \mathrm { n M }$ for cationic miniprotein ZF5.3 (16) and $2 5 3 \mathrm { ~ \ n M }$ for hydrocarbon-stapled peptide SAH-p53-8.

[Introduction] Background 
The main reasons for the increasing interest in permeable peptides are the inability of small molecules and biologics to interfere with complex intracellular targets, and the potential to apply peptides as substitutes for biologics, for example, via the oral route. Evidence for these developments was discussed in a recent review on intracellular delivery of peptides [1]. Cell penetrating peptides (CPPs) and technologies, how to identify transport-active peptides have been described in this contribution detailing stapled peptides able to block intracellular protein–protein interactions and other cyclic peptides shown to be orally bioavailable. Some achievements with respect to conjugation and formulation technologies have also been addressed in this communication. Interesting new findings on CPPs relate to studies of a combination of a cyclic CPP and a cyclic cargo into a bicyclic construct. Due to enhanced endosomal escape the CPP, cyclo (Phe-2-Nal-Arg-Arg-ArgArg-Gln) (1), results in an improved uptake than achieved with classical transport-active peptides like Tat, as judged by detection of cargo in the cytoplasm and the nucleus [2]. Another new finding was reported by Pellois using a dimeric Tat-peptide (df TAT) [3]. This larger peptide seems to overcome the well-known obstacle of entrapment of molecules in endosomes/lysosomes. According to quantification by fluorescence, the study clearly demonstrated the superiority of df TAT, and using uptake inhibitors as appropriate controls, helped to gain mechanistic insight. Since endosomal lysis can be extremely toxic, for example, by leakage of endosomal/lysomal proteases, a remarkable aspect of this delivery vehicle is the minimal cellular responses associated with the endosomal leakage observed during the duration of these experiments. In particular the latter study provides evidence, how to incorporate our current understanding and known modulators in the design of the experiments to arrive at unambiguous conclusions. Overall these examples indicate the potential to expand our knowledge regarding modifications enabling release from endosomes/ lysosomes, and thus, how to come up with sufficiently high cytosolic peptide concentration to efficiently address intracellular targets. However, the focus of this contribution is more on recent insights regarding methodologies to support the assessment of permeability, and structural modifications proven or thought to provide a path forward to permeable cyclic peptides rather than conjugation strategies.
